F002.name: Photos and PDFs sent to Happy are read and answered
F002.description: Send a photo of a flyer, label or receipt, or a PDF packet, and Happy reads it and answers questions about it; today a message that is only an attachment is dropped without a reply. Nothing on the Mac screens what a parent sends: the photo or PDF goes to the cloud model as it is, which Tony accepted on 12 Oct. The house rule goes on the printed sheet: no bank, tax or medical papers.
F002.example: A parent sends a photo of a school flyer from the third-grader's class and asks 'what do we need to send in, and by when?' Happy answers in the same thread.
F002.how: One switch: `channels.imessage.includeAttachments: true`. Photos then go to the reply model as images, and an attached PDF arrives as extracted text. The same deploy sets `tools.media.audio.enabled: false`, so audio understanding stays off until the voice card (F003) lists a transcriber on the Mac. In each parent's AGENTS.md the line that says Happy cannot see photos or files is replaced and a line says it cannot watch video; the smoke-eval check that forbids asking for an upload changes to match. A suggested layout for a flyer or form, to change after the first real ones: the dates, what to do, any money or form, the deadline, and which child if that matters; no line count. One planted-file test: a PDF and a photo with hidden instructions must cause no tool call, a hand-off to the web helper, a mail lookup, and a fetch or mail read by the parent's own agent included. One line goes on the printed sheet. No gate plugin; no house-rules rule.
caveats: Nothing screens what a parent sends: any photo or PDF goes to the cloud model as it is. The only guard against a statement sent by mistake is the house rule on the printed sheet.

The same switch also lets voice memos and video in, and audio auto-detection tries a configured provider key before any local program, so audio understanding is set off in the same deploy and stays off until the voice card (F003) lists a transcriber on the Mac.
Happy cannot watch video on this provider set, so an AGENTS.md line has it say so and ask for a photo or a few screenshots.

store:false covers less than it reads: OpenAI can keep abuse-monitoring logs, content included, for up to 30 days unless the organisation has Zero Data Retention, and family photos fall under that. Tony accepted this on 12 Oct.
Medical papers are on the 'do not send' line, so the medical-bill reply layout is not built.
Only the switch is built: the optional `pdf` tool (page selection) is not part of this form.
corrections: Catalog JSON 'needs' says view_image is already granted and sets agents.defaults.pdfModel to luna. The minimal profile contains only session_status and gateway (tool-policy.md:36), and pdfModel is an agents.defaults key that is unset by default (pdf.md:124). The Markdown already drops both.
unverified: Reading accuracy on blurry phone photos and scanned image-only PDFs was not measured.
The exact point at which an inbound PDF falls back to page images; the 200-characters-per-page rule is documented for the pdf tool, not for channel attachments.
That the gateway process under the happy account already has Full Disk Access to the Messages attachments folder comes from the 9 Oct notes and was not re-checked.
Whether OpenClaw treats the per-person custom provider ids exactly like the stock OpenAI provider for image input was not tested live (the config repo does declare image input for both models).
What a voice memo turns into with audio understanding off has not been seen on a live turn; the go-live check is that it is declined and no audio leaves the Mac.

The eval endpoint is documented to take images; whether a PDF can be handed to an eval-only copy the same way has not been tried, so the planted PDF may have to be a supervised turn from Tony's phone.
F002.safety: A photo or PDF is outside content read directly by the agent that holds a parent's chats. That agent replies only in its own chat. It is allowed the fetch tool and, where the lookup is on, the Gmail read tools, only so that its helpers can use them, and is told never to call them itself; reminders (F007), where live, are pinned to the asker in code. The hand-off to the web helper (F019), the roadmap's one remaining leak path, and a fetch or mail read by that agent itself have only prompt rules and the planted-file test until the house-rules plugin's check exists.

F003.name: Voice memos to Happy, transcribed on the Mac mini, with a spoken reply in the built-in Mac voice
F003.description: A parent sends a voice memo instead of typing; the Mac mini transcribes it, echoes the text back and answers, and the answer also arrives as an audio file in the built-in Mac voice. Speech is turned into text on the Mac mini, and the transcript then goes to the cloud model like any typed message. A parent can already dictate with the iPhone keyboard, so this is a convenience.
F003.example: A parent sends a voice memo: 'will it rain tomorrow morning?' Happy echoes the transcript, answers in text and attaches the same answer as audio. Or Tony sends `/tts latest` after a long answer and gets it read out.
F003.how: In: an explicit `tools.media.models` CLI entry for `whisper-cli` (audio capability, `{{AttachmentPath}}`), with `tools.media.audio.enabled: true` and `tools.media.audio.echoTranscript: true`. It needs Homebrew whisper.cpp, ffmpeg and a GGML model file, installed from the admin account; OpenClaw converts the memo to WAV itself. With an explicit entry, auto-detection, which tries a configured provider key first, is not used. Out: the `tts` block with provider `tts-local-cli` running the macOS `say` command, `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false` and no cloud speech provider; `tts.auto: "inbound"` on the two parents' own agents only, so a voice memo gets a spoken answer as an audio file and every other agent stays text-only; `/tts latest` on demand, for Tony. The AGENTS.md line that says Happy cannot hear voice memos is replaced. First test: one live voice-memo turn whose trace shows the transcript, not the audio file, reaching the cloud model. No plugin; no rule in the house-rules plugin.
caveats: A parent can already dictate a message with the iPhone keyboard and send it as text, so for the two adults this is a convenience and not a new ability.

Local-only is not the default in either direction: audio auto-detection tries a configured provider key before any local program, and the keyless Microsoft online voice is on by default and can serve as a fallback, so the transcriber is listed explicitly and the Microsoft voice is switched off. `/tts provider <id>` changes the provider for everyone, so having no cloud speech provider configured is the control, and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs, a cloud voice) stays off.
The reply is a plain audio file attachment (WAV, several megabytes for a few minutes), not a voice bubble; the voice-bubble option belongs to the Private API actions, which need SIP off.
Long replies are summarised by the cloud chat model before they are spoken, or cut short.

`/tts latest` and the other /tts commands work for Tony only: Jordan is not on the command list, and OpenClaw silently ignores /tts from her. The spoken reply after a voice memo does not depend on it.
Talk mode in the iPhone app (OCL-01) has its own speech setting and does not pick up this voice automatically.
corrections: Markdown pairs a whisper-cpp install with audio.preferredModel: "cli:whisper". The matcher compares that value with cli: plus the entry's exact command string (dist/resolve-KJuMET3H.mjs:148), so for whisper-cpp it must be cli:whisper-cli, or cli: plus the full path used in the entry; cli:whisper only matches the Python whisper CLI.

The Homebrew formula is now named whisper.cpp (formerly whisper-cpp) and its page says GGML model files are not downloaded by default. The 9 Oct note about a model that downloads automatically describes the Python whisper CLI (media-understanding.md:168), not whisper-cli.

ffmpeg is a hard requirement the Markdown leaves out: upstream whisper-cli reads only 16-bit WAV (github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp README), OpenClaw shells out to ffmpeg for that conversion (dist/ffmpeg-exec-VIr-PIWC.mjs:25 prints the brew install hint), and the formula does not pull ffmpeg in.
unverified: The container format of iMessage voice memos, and whether ffmpeg decodes it cleanly, were not tested.
Transcription speed on the M5 Pro was not measured.

That only the transcript reaches the cloud model: the media docs say the original attachment is still passed to the model, and the model's listed inputs are text and image, so the audio file should be left out, but this was not checked on a live turn.

Whether the per-person custom provider ids count as OpenAI audio auth in auto-detection is undocumented; the explicit CLI entry is meant to sidestep the question, and the first live turn shows whether it does.

Whether a failed local synthesis can still fall through to the Microsoft online voice once that provider is switched off; the docs say other configured providers are fallbacks and that Microsoft is enabled by default. Not tested.
That the documented say preset writes a valid WAV on macOS 27 without extra data-format flags was not run.
How Messages on iPhone presents a WAV attachment (inline player or plain file) was not tested.
The 1,500-character summarise-or-truncate threshold is documented (tts/commands.md:104) but its effect on long replies here was not tried.
That the spoken reply after a voice memo reaches a parent who is not on the command list was read from the docs and not tried from Jordan's phone.
F003.safety: Speech is turned into text on the Mac mini; the transcript goes to the cloud model like any typed message, and the first live turn checks that the audio file is withheld. The spoken reply is made on the Mac, with the Microsoft voice off and no cloud speech provider. A voice memo comes from an allowlisted parent and brings no outside content.

F007.name: Timed reminders over iMessage, one-off and repeating (Tony only)
F007.description: 'Remind me at 4:30 to pick up the kids', or a repeating reminder, becomes a scheduled text to the asker, and reminders can be listed and cancelled; to change one, cancel it and set a new one. It works for Tony only: OpenClaw lets only a command owner use the scheduling tool from chat, and Jordan is not one, so she uses the Reminders app or Siri on her own phone.
F007.example: Tony texts: 'Remind me at 4:30 to pick up the kids.' At 4:30 he gets a text from Happy: 'Pick up the kids.' Later he texts 'what reminders do I have?' and then 'cancel the 4:30 one'.
F007.how: First T7, with `cron.triggers.enabled: false` already set: one throwaway reminder created from iMessage on a throwaway agent with no memory, accounts or other tools, removed in the same sitting. Then T5 for the scheduling tool: a logging plugin shows which fields the blocking check is given. Then the reminder rule in the house-rules plugin: add only, as a text to the asker, no web address, an empty tool list; list and remove allowed; update and run refused; blocked when the check itself fails. Then the roadmap's recipient test: five ways to change the recipient, the other parent included. Only then is the `automations` tool granted, to Tony's agent alone, in the agent's tool list and the sandbox's. One-shot reminders delete themselves after delivery; repeating ones carry the time zone. One instruction: when 'remind me' is unclear, ask. The smoke-eval case that expects 'I can't set reminders' is replaced by a reminder case.
caveats: For a plain personal timer, Siri and the iPhone Reminders app already do the job, including reminders tied to a place. Happy's version earns its place for reminders that come out of something Happy just read or answered, such as a flyer's dates (F010).

It works for Tony only: OpenClaw refuses the scheduling tool to a sender who is not a command owner, whatever the config says, and Tony is the only owner. Jordan uses the Reminders app or Siri on her own phone.
A reminder cannot be edited in place: the rule refuses any change to an existing job, so Tony cancels it and sets a new one.

Tony's agent can list every scheduled job on the gateway, Jordan's morning mail text included, and can remove one. The rule stops it changing or running them; a removal is written to the scheduler's admin log, and the job is then created again with the jobs script. Reminders are the one kind of job the jobs script does not create.
Once the shared Reminders list (F030) exists, 'remind me' can mean a text from Happy at a set time (this card) or an item on that list, so the agent is told to ask when it is unclear.

The card rests on T7, which has not been run: the installed docs describe creating a job from chat for Control UI administrators, not for an iMessage owner turn. If T7 fails, the rule and the grant are not built and Tony decides what comes next.
corrections: Catalog JSON 'needs' lists --delete-after-run. One-shot --at jobs already delete themselves after confirmed delivery (how-it-works.md:19). The Markdown already says so.
unverified: Creating a reminder from an iMessage owner turn has not been tried live on this install; managing-jobs.md:81 describes chat creation for Control UI administrators (T7).
Whether the blocking check is called for the scheduling tool, and which fields carry a job's target, its other destinations and its tool list, has not been tried (T5).
That a job created by the agent can be given an empty tool list by the creating turn, and that the rule can require it, was read from the docs and not tried.

The comparison with Siri and Apple Reminders for one-off personal timers was not sourced.
F007.safety: OpenClaw advises keeping the scheduling tool off agents that read outside content, because it can name where a job's text goes, a web address included. Tony's agent gets it only after the reminder rule is live in code: add only, to the asker alone, no web address, an empty tool list, blocked when the check fails. Script triggers stay off.

F009.name: Shared Google calendar, read-only: 'what's on Saturday?' and 'is Friday at 1 clear?'
F009.description: 'What's on Saturday?' or 'is Friday at 1 clear?' is answered from the family's shared Google calendar, read-only; nothing on the calendar is changed. 'Clear' means nothing shows on the calendars the asking parent's own sign-in can see; the other parent's own calendars are not read, so Happy cannot say whether both parents are free. The same connection feeds the 21:00 evening text (F014).
F009.example: A parent texts: 'What's on Saturday?' and gets the day's events from the shared calendar. Tony asks 'is Friday at 1 clear?' and gets what his own sign-in shows for that hour; nothing on the calendar is changed.
F009.how: One host-side stdio MCP server per parent. Sign-in: `gog auth add <account> --services calendar --readonly`, approved by that parent on Google's screen and stored apart from the mail sign-in, so the grant covers Calendar only. Server: `gog --account <account> mcp --allow-tool calendar_events`, because by default the server registers every read tool, mail and Drive search included. Each parent's own agent allows only its own calendar server's tool by name, in the agent's tool list and the sandbox's, and denies the other parent's; `bundle-mcp` is not opened. 'Is Friday at 1 clear?' is answered by listing that hour's events with the same tool; there is no free/busy tool. No rule of its own: the house-rules plugin's account-connector rule (a person's connector answers only that person's agents, blocked when the check fails) is live before the server is granted. One eval case: an event title that carries instructions must cause no tool call, a hand-off to the web helper included.
caveats: 'Is Friday at 1 clear?' is answered only from events the asking parent's sign-in can see: the shared calendar, and that parent's own calendars unless the tool can be pinned to one calendar. 'Clear' does not mean both parents are free. gog's server offers one calendar tool, the events list, and no free/busy tool; reading each parent's own calendar as busy-only belongs to the conflict watch (MKT-06).
Happy does not write to the calendar. A date from a flyer or an email is in calendar answers, and in the evening text, only after a parent adds the event on the phone.

A renewal, expiry or upkeep date is one calendar event with an alert that a parent types once on the shared calendar (a repeating event for upkeep). It then shows in calendar answers and the evening text, and the phone's own alert works when Happy is down. There is no renewals table and no monthly 'coming due' text.

A public feed (the school district's calendar, a team schedule, library events) shows up in calendar answers only after the shared Google calendar is subscribed to its link, which Google allows from a computer browser only; Google gives no refresh interval, and TeamSnap says changes can take up to 24 hours to appear.

Two layers keep one parent's calendar out of the other parent's agent: tool permissions with an explicit deny (checked by T2), and the coded account-connector rule. Tony accepted going without the second layer for mail only, so here it is in place first. If T5 shows the blocking check is never called for a connector's tools, the rule cannot be written and Tony decides whether one layer is enough for the calendar too.
corrections: The 9 Oct wording has Tony hand-write the calendar MCP server. gogcli.sh/mcp.html documents a built-in stdio server (gog --account <account> mcp) with a read-only calendar_events tool and an --allow-tool filter, so listing events needs no custom code. Freebusy and conflicts exist only as CLI commands (gogcli.sh/commands) and still need a wrapper.

Catalog JSON 'needs' expects a calendar.readonly scope from --services calendar. The documented switch is --readonly on gog auth add; Google's scope list does include calendar.readonly (developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/auth). The Markdown asked to verify the flag; gog's command page confirms it.
unverified: That `--services calendar` with `--readonly` yields a calendar-only read grant, and that `--allow-tool calendar_events` leaves no other tool registered, were read from gogcli.sh and not run; `gog mcp --list-tools` is the check once gog is installed.

Whether a second sign-in for the same Google account, stored apart (the wave A runbook keeps each sign-in in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own, through its wrapper; gog's --home or --client switch alone would not separate them), replaces or widens the mail sign-in; gog's auth page does not say (T2).
That the minimal tool profile plus a per-agent allow exposes exactly one account server: the roadmap lists it as not yet confirmed on this version (T2).
Whether the blocking check is called for a connector's tools at all, and which fields it is given (T5).
Whether gog's calendar_events tool can be pinned to a single calendar id was not confirmed.
That events from a URL-subscribed calendar are returned through the Google Calendar API, and so through gog, was not confirmed.
Whether the school district, clubs and library the family uses publish feed links was not checked.
F009.safety: Read-only and calendar-only: each sign-in covers Calendar alone, apart from the mail sign-in; the server offers only the events tool, to its owner's agent alone, held there by tool permissions and the coded connector rule. Outsiders can write event titles, so calendar text is outside content; that agent is told not to fetch pages itself (it holds the fetch tool only for the web helper, and the house-rules rule blocks it if T5 allows that rule), and its one way out is the hand-off to the web helper (F019).

F019.name: Research helper: answers from public web pages with the link and the time fetched
F019.description: Happy can read public web pages that load without JavaScript or a login: a research helper with no memory, no accounts and no family data fetches the page, and the parent's own agent relays the answer with its link and the time it was fetched. When a page cannot be read, Happy says 'could not verify'. Nothing the helper fetches can reach the home network.
F019.example: A parent texts: 'What time does the town pool open on Saturday? Check their site.' Happy sends the hours with the link and when the page was fetched.
F019.how: First T4: one hand-off from Tony's agent to the helper, with a time limit, must return its answer in the same chat while agents still cannot see each other's sessions. Agent: a shared `research` agent from the family file: a fresh sandbox per conversation, memory search off, no accounts, `web_search` and `web_fetch` only, its own capped key. Each parent's agent adds `research` to its `subagents.allowAgents`, beside its own mail reader; `sessions_spawn` and `subagents.requireAgentId: true` are already set by the mail lookup, or are set here if the lookup is off; the time limit is the gateway-wide `agents.defaults.subagents.runTimeoutSeconds`, because 2026.9.7 rejects that key under one agent. Under the pattern Tony said on 13 Oct he expects to adopt for every helper, each parent's agent is also allowed `web_fetch`, which it is denied today (in its tool list and its sandbox tool list): on 2026.9.7 an agent started by another keeps only the tools its asker is allowed (the asker's allowed tools and its denies are passed to the helper and applied last), so the helper could not fetch otherwise. The helper's own list, `web_search` and `web_fetch`, is what narrows the hand-off. Guardrails: both `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` keys unset, `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, no fetch-provider plugin, `tools.web.fetch.useTrustedEnvProxy` off, `browser.enabled: false`, `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. One rule in the helper's AGENTS.md: give the link and the time fetched, show the page's own date when it has one, give a price or date only from a fetched page, say 'could not verify'. In each parent's AGENTS.md the 'cannot open links' line becomes the hand-off rule: never fetch a page yourself, hand it to the helper, and what a task may carry; its smoke-eval case changes too. Four planted eval cases; in each, a fetch by the parent's own agent counts as a failure. Tony's agent first, Jordan's a day later. No plugin and no house-rules rule in this wave; when the house-rules plugin is created in wave C (planned there by Tony's choice of 13 Oct to keep the wave order), its who-may-call rule also covers `web_fetch` on a parent's own agent, if test T5 shows that the check is told which agent is calling; otherwise an instruction and the tool-call record stay the only guard.
caveats: The plain fetch runs no JavaScript and cannot log in, so such pages stay unread until the extra readers (F020) exist, and Happy says 'could not verify'. A slow lookup gets no 'on it' and no plain-words 'cancel that': the helper's built-in finish report is the only progress message, and a lookup ends at its time limit or at Tony's built-in stop.

If the hand-off test (T4) fails, the only documented alternative is session visibility `tree` for the whole gateway, which changes a signed-off setting and needs Tony's yes plus a re-run of the separation check.

The home-network block rests on the fetch tool resolving and pinning the address itself, so `tools.web.fetch.useTrustedEnvProxy` stays off and both private-network keys stay truly unset: an explicitly written `false` on the browser key turns hostname navigation into an allowlist and would stop the later research browser (F020).

Once the helper can fetch pages, neither the firewall nor the proxy can hold the gateway program to a list of hosts; they refuse home-network addresses and nothing more, so tool permissions, not the firewall, keep the mail readers and the shared agents off the web; a parent's own agent is allowed the fetch tool so that the helper can use it, and there an instruction and the planted tests do that work.

The answer rule and the rule on what goes into a task (the town and the children's ages yes, names and the school no) are prompt rules; nothing mechanical enforces them, and the planted eval cases are the only check. The roadmap's prompt-injection tripwire is not built with this card: by Tony's answer of 12 Oct it waits for local models.

The fetch tool's home-network check covers `web_fetch` only, so host-side helpers that take a web address (the summarize wrapper, watcher scripts) need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks.
corrections: The 9 Oct verifier notes advised turning the sandbox off for research; the installed docs say a sandboxed requester cannot spawn an unsandboxed target, so the catalog's final wording (keep mode all) is the only workable one.
A verifier note asked for research rules in AGENTS.md and SOUL.md; the installed docs say sub-agents keep only AGENTS.md, so every citation and no-login rule must be in that one file.

13 Oct: the card had each parent's agent denied `web_fetch` while its helper fetched. The installed code passes the asker's allowed tools and denies to the helper (dist/sessions-spawn-tool-B5tfhM3J.mjs:3244), so the asker must be allowed the tool as well.
unverified: That a cross-agent hand-off returns its result with agent-to-agent messaging off and session visibility set to self: the roadmap lists this as untested on 2026.9.7, and nothing was run here (T4).
The rule on what may go into the task text is a prompt rule; nothing mechanical enforces what a parent's agent writes into it.
Nothing in the installed stack enforces citations; it is a prompt rule the model can ignore, and the eval cases are the only check.
Whether page fetches pass through the outbound proxy once it is configured: the installed docs point both ways and nothing has been tried; it is read from the proxy's log when the gate is built.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.
How long a real lookup takes: nothing on the current stack runs longer than about 20 seconds, so whether an 'on it' line is ever needed is unknown until the hand-off exists.

That a helper started by a parent's agent that is allowed `web_fetch` keeps `web_search` and `web_fetch` and nothing else: read from the installed code, and first tried with the mail lookup in wave A (T4).

That a parent's own agent, allowed `web_fetch` for the hand-off, never fetches a page itself: an instruction, checked by the planted cases and its tool-call record, not a limit until wave C, and then only if T5 allows the coded rule.
F019.safety: The helper reads untrusted pages but holds no memory, accounts or family data, and cannot reach the home network. The roadmap's one remaining leak path stays open: a parent's agent holds private chats and writes the task text for a helper that can fetch any public address. A prompt rule and planted tests guard it; the helper's answer is treated as untrusted. Under that pattern the path is one step shorter: the parent's own agent is itself allowed the fetch tool, because a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, and only its instructions and the planted tests keep it from fetching a page itself until the house-rules plugin's check exists in wave C, and after that only if test T5 allowed it.

F030.name: Shared Apple Reminders list: Happy reads it, adds to it and ticks items off
F030.description: Happy can read, add to and tick off items on the Apple Reminders list the two parents share, so a change shows up on both phones. Tony names the list at execution. Nothing is coded until a by-hand test shows that an item added from the Mac reaches that list on both phones.
F030.example: After Happy answers 'what do I need for pancakes for six?', a parent texts 'add the flour, eggs and buttermilk to our list'. The three items appear on the shared list on both parents' phones. Later the other parent texts 'what's still on the list?' and gets the open items.
F030.how: First T9, by hand, before any code: in happy's desktop session join the list Tony names, add and tick off one item with `remindctl`, and look at both phones; then add one item with a due time and note whether a phone alerts. If the item does not arrive, try a list that Happy's account owns and shares to both parents; if that fails too, the card is dropped. Then an in-house host-side tool plugin wrapping `remindctl` with three verbs (list, add, complete) on that one list only, no delete and no due dates, allowed on both parents' own agents in the agent's tool list and the sandbox's. Reminders access is granted once by hand in the gateway's own process context. One instruction: when 'remind me' could mean a timed text or a list item, ask. No house-rules rule: the tool's three verbs and its one list, fixed in its configuration, are the limit in code.
caveats: For a single item spoken to the phone, Siri already creates reminders with nothing to build. The bridge earns its place when the items come out of something Happy read or planned (a recipe link, the dinner plan in F033, a flyer).
If T9 fails for a list a parent owns, the fallback is a list that Happy's account owns and shares to both parents; if that fails too, the card is dropped.
The tool sets no due dates and cannot delete: an item added by mistake is ticked off, or removed on the phone. T9 notes whether a due time alerts a phone, in case a parent later asks for dated items.
Who sees the list is set in Apple's sharing, not in Happy's code. What one parent's agent adds is seen by the other parent, and by anyone else the list is ever shared with.
A shared Apple Note as a second filing target is not part of this build.
A scheduled text of the open list is not built; if a parent asks for one and names the day and hour, it is one more job in the jobs script.
unverified: No opened source confirms that remindctl can add to or complete items on a shared iCloud list owned by another family member; its README only says reminders sync through the normal iCloud path (T9).
Which binary macOS records the Reminders permission against when the launchd gateway spawns remindctl is not documented in any opened source; it needs one test on happy's logged-in desktop.
Whether a due time on an item added from the Mac alerts a parent's phone on a shared list (the second half of T9).
F030.safety: The tool can only list, add and complete on the one list fixed in its configuration; the model cannot write elsewhere or delete. An added item shows on every phone the list is shared with, and Happy's code cannot check the sharing, so Tony confirms at execution that only the two parents share it. List text typed by anyone on the list is outside content.

F031.name: Household database: shared rows for the dose log and the coverage planner
F031.description: A small database on the Mac mini that both parents' agents read and write, so either parent gets the same answer whoever entered the row. It is built only as far as two planned features need it: one table for the sick-day dose log (CRT-10) and one for the childcare coverage grid (CRT-11). It has no general 'save a fact' tools: reference text both parents look up lives in the family handbook (F043), and each parent's own notes stay with that parent (F041).
F031.example: One parent texts Happy what they gave the kindergartner and when. Later the other parent asks 'when was the last dose logged?' and gets the same row, with who logged it. In the same way, one parent texts that a no-school week is covered, and the other parent's 'which weeks are still open?' no longer lists it.
F031.how: One in-house tool plugin over Node's built-in `node:sqlite`, with one database file on the Mac mini. It sits in the config repo's `plugins/` folder like the weather plugin: the ordinary deploy copies it and it loads from `plugins.load.paths` after a restart. No general tools: no schedule tools and no `fact_get` or `fact_set`. Each feature adds one table and its own typed tools: the dose log (CRT-10) and the coverage grid (CRT-11). Every input is typed and short in the tool's own schema (a date or time, a whole number, a choice from a fixed list, a label of at most about 40 characters); no separate secret detector. The tools are allowed by name on the two parents' own agents (`tools.alsoAllow` and the sandbox gate `tools.sandbox.tools`) and on no shared agent or mail reader. A scheduled job that reads a table lists the tool by the name the plugin declares. No house-rules rule is added.
caveats: Everything in it is shared between the two adults on purpose: neither table filters by person. That steps outside 'one data domain per person', by Tony's pick of the two features on 12 Oct. Something meant for one parent belongs in that parent's own notes (F041).
Only two tables are planned. There is no general upkeep or 'when is the filter due?' table: a repeating date is a calendar event or a reminder.
A later feature that needs rows both parents' agents write adds its own table and typed tools here; it does not start a second store.

Inputs are short and typed, with no secret detector, so a short secret typed as a label would be stored; the standing instruction never to ask for or reveal passwords, keys or codes is the only guard against that.

The dose table holds what was given to a child, and that text goes to the cloud model whenever a parent's agent reads it back. Tony picked the dose log knowing this, and its card (CRT-10) carries his confirm step at execution.
The rows can be read only through Happy: when the Mac mini or the cloud model is down, neither parent can get at them.
corrections: The 9 Oct verifier note says the secret-rejecting before_tool_call hook can live in the same plugin as the defineToolPlugin store. docs/plugins/tool-plugins.md:11 says defineToolPlugin adds tools only, and :233 points to definePluginEntry when tools are combined with hooks.

The catalog chooses defineToolPlugin for the store but still names its tools home-store__schedule_* in the automations. docs/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools.md:242 gives that server__tool form to MCP servers only; a plugin's tools carry the names it declares, so job tool lists must use those.
unverified: node:sqlite is labelled release candidate on nodejs.org; no long-run test of it inside the gateway process was done.

That a tool in this plugin is told which agent called it, so a row can carry who wrote it without asking the model: the installed tool-context type lists the calling agent's id and the sender's id (dist/agent-harness-runtime-BbN1SctJ.d.ts), and the docs show that context reaching a tool built through a factory (plugins/tool-plugins.md:138); not tried on a live turn.

Which plugin form is used: the card named `defineToolPlugin`, which the installed docs describe as a TypeScript package with a build step (plugins/tool-plugins.md:20), while the one plugin in the config repo is plain JavaScript written with `definePluginEntry` and `api.registerTool`. Settled at execution.
Where the database file is kept so that the nightly backup includes it and a restore brings it back: not tried.

That the tools are offered to the two parents' agents and to no other agent or its eval-only copy: the separation check is extended to them at execution. The parents' own eval-only copies are generated with the same tool list as the parents' agents, so what a test run may write into the real file is settled then.
F031.safety: Both parents' agents read and write the same rows, so the store is shared between the two adults on purpose. Its tools are allowed by name on those two agents only. The tool's own schema keeps every input short and typed, which leaves a planted instruction little room to persist. No send and no web access is added.

F041.name: Saved notes: 'remember this' goes to that parent's own notes and is found again by keyword
F041.description: A parent texts 'remember that...' and their own agent saves the line to that parent's own notes and says what it saved. In a later chat the note is found by searching for its words; it is not in view at the start of a chat, and Happy saves nothing a parent did not ask it to save. Each parent's notes stay with that parent: the other parent's agent cannot find them.
F041.example: A parent texts: 'Remember that the library books are due back on the 20th.' A week later, in a new chat, the same parent asks 'when are the library books due?' and Happy finds the note and answers. The other parent's agent cannot find it.
F041.how: T6 runs first, on Tony's eval-only copy. Then the generator gives each parent's agent `write` and `edit` (also in the sandbox tool gate), with `apply_patch` denied by name and `read` left denied, plus `memory_search` and `memory_get`, keyword-only (`memory.search.provider: "none"`, already set). The sandbox stays closed to the agent folder (`workspaceAccess: "none"`), so a note lands in a notes folder inside the agent's own sandbox workspace; that folder is added to that agent's own search paths (`agents.entries.<id>.memory.search.extraPaths`, never the global list). Instructions: save only what the parent asked, in the parent's words; say what was saved; do not save a child's health details. Not built: a read-write workspace, tracking of web tool calls, the session-memory hook, any copy of notes outside the agent, search by meaning. House-rules plugin: no rule when T6 passes. The separation canaries are extended to memory search.
caveats: A saved note is found only when the agent searches for it: it is not in view at the start of a chat, and a scheduled text or a hand-off to a helper does not know it.

Notes are found by their words, not their meaning, so a question worded differently from the note may miss it. Search by meaning (an embedding model on the Mac mini, a deliverable of the roadmap's local-models milestone, which Tony has put off) and OpenClaw's Active Memory recall stay later options that are Tony's call; neither is part of this build.
Notes belong to one parent. A fact both parents should get the same answer to goes into the family file (F042) or the family handbook (F043), both typed by Tony.

No refusal is built for a 'remember' in a turn that also carried web results. OpenClaw is expected to label such a note untrusted by itself, T6 records what actually happens, and a prompt rule plus a behaviour test are what stand against a planted 'remember this'.
There is no undo and no copy of note text anywhere else. A parent asks 'what did you save about me?' to read their notes back; the weekly text (G006) only lists which note files changed.

The design rests on T6, which has not been run, and it has to pass for Jordan as she is, a non-owner. If it fails for her, notes go live for Tony first while a fix is found. If it fails outright, the fallback left is the original design (a read-write agent folder plus one house-rules rule that keeps writes inside the notes folder), which reverses two signed-off settings; Tony says yes or no to it at execution.
corrections: The catalog relies on `sessions_search` with visibility `agent` to find pre-reset conversations. docs/gateway/config-tools/sessions-and-subagents.md:58 says a sandboxed session stays limited to sessions it spawned while agents.defaults.sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility is 'spawned' (the default); the mains run with sandbox mode all, so that key must change as well. docs/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools.md:372 adds that tools.sessions.visibility is gateway-wide, not per agent.

The catalog ties this to M2 (local models). docs/plugins/llama-cpp.md:123 documents an embedding-only setup that adds no chat model, so the text leg does not depend on M2 and can be done on the installed stack.

The 9 Oct reason for dropping photo search is that no local multimodal embedder exists. Google's EmbeddingGemma page now describes EmbeddingGemma 2 as multimodal and local; the actual block is that OpenClaw 2026.9.7 only indexes images with gemini-embedding-2 (docs/reference/memory-config.md:495).
unverified: T6 has not been run: that `write` and `edit`, with the sandbox closed to the agent folder, can save a note into a folder inside the sandbox workspace; that memory search finds it there through a per-agent extra path; and that it survives a sandbox rebuild and is in the nightly backup.

Whether a note saved in one of Jordan's turns (she is not the command owner) comes back from memory search like any other note, or is shown to the model with an untrusted label: the installed code records a non-owner's write as untrusted (dist/agent-tools-D5UK6LHM.mjs:496); not seen on a live turn.
How a note saved in a turn that carried web content is recorded, and whether it is then found only by search: read in the installed docs and code (memory-architecture.md:117 and :215), not tried.
That a long chat writes no note by itself while the sandbox has no workspace access: concepts/memory.md says the automatic memory flush is skipped then; checked once in T6.

That the file tools can be split as planned: they are denied as one group today and a deny wins over an allow, so the generator names them one by one; whether `edit` works on a note while `read` stays denied is seen in T6.
Notes kept outside the agent folder carry the platform's 'untrusted' origin label; T6 has to show that this does not hide them from search.
For the fallback after a failed T6: whether a plugin's blocking check is given the path of a file write (the file-write turn of T5).
F041.safety: Notes stay in the parent's own agent. The write tools reach only that agent's own sandbox folder, so they cannot change its rules file or the rendered family facts; shared agents and mail readers have no memory search. A note is where a planted instruction could persist, so a planted 'remember this' must save nothing in five runs of five.

F042.name: Family facts from the family file, known to each parent's agent in every chat
F042.description: Tony types the family facts he wants Happy to know into the family file: to start with, the two children, their school years and the school district. After the next deploy both parents' agents begin every one-to-one chat already knowing them, so nobody has to explain who 'the third-grader' is. The facts are not rendered into the web helper, the mail readers or any shared agent.
F042.example: In a fresh chat a parent texts: 'write a two-line absence note for our third-grader for Friday.' Happy drafts it with the child's first name and the school district, which nobody typed in that chat, and the parent sends it themselves.
F042.how: One generator step. New fields in family.json5 hold the facts Tony types; gen-family.mjs renders them through new template placeholders into files it already writes for each parent's own agent: USER.md while they fit under its 4,000-character cap, otherwise a section of AGENTS.md. The generator does not start writing MEMORY.md, which stays with OpenClaw and the eval marker (the deploy script never touches it), and no trigger comments are used. Nothing is rendered into the bootstrap files of the web helper, the mail readers or any shared agent; a scheduled job that needs a fact carries it in its own message. No reply-language line is rendered. No tool, no send path and no house-rules rule is added. Once the web helper (F019) exists, its hand-off canary is run with the real facts present.
caveats: USER.md has a 4,000-character cap that everything rendered into it shares, so the list has to stay short; what does not fit goes into a section of AGENTS.md and takes prompt space in every session of that parent's agent.
Rendered facts change only when Tony edits the family file and redeploys; a parent cannot change one by text. What a parent tells Happy in chat goes to that parent's own saved notes (F041).
The typed facts, the children's names and school among them, are sent to the cloud model at the start of every chat of each parent's own agent.
Children's health details are not typed into the family file: that is the default Tony kept, and the dose log (CRT-10) is the one planned feature that holds any.
Each parent's agent can search the web today. The default Tony kept (a search may use the town and the children's ages, never their names or the school) is a prompt rule, not an enforced limit.
Whether a scheduled run loads the rendered file has not been tried on a live job, so a scheduled text that needs a fact carries it in its own message.
corrections: A 9 Oct verifier note says there is no per-language voice switch. tts/output.md:56 documents one for the bundled Microsoft provider, which is an online service; it does not help the offline say path.
unverified: Whether a scheduled run loads USER.md was not tried on a live job: the installed code lists it among the files a scheduled run gets and leaves MEMORY.md out (dist/workspace-DmDIneFk.mjs:742), while the scheduler guide only says a job does not infer a reply language (cron-jobs/delivery.md:140).
Whether the facts Tony wants fit under USER.md's 4,000-character cap is unknown until he types them, and the overflow route into a section of AGENTS.md has not been tried.

That a parent's agent keeps a child's name and the school out of a web search and out of a task for the web helper is a behaviour, tested by the hand-off canary; it has never been run with real facts present.
F042.safety: The rendered files go only into the two parents' own agents, never into the web helper, a mail reader or a shared agent. They hold the children's names and school and go to the cloud model with every chat; children's health details stay out. No tool or send path is added, and the hand-off canary is re-run with real facts present.

F043.name: Family handbook: shared pages Tony types that both parents' agents can search
F043.description: One shared family handbook that both parents' agents can search: plain pages Tony types, such as appliance details and who services what, plus the reference pages other planned cards read. Either parent asks and gets the same stored answer. Happy does not write or change pages; a parent who wants something added tells Tony.
F043.example: Made up to show the feature: suppose Tony has typed a page listing appliance model numbers and repair contacts. Jordan asks 'who do we call about the dishwasher?' and gets the contact from that page; Tony would get the same answer.
F043.how: One shared Markdown folder on the Mac mini, outside both parents' workspaces. Tony types the pages in the config repo, and the ordinary deploy, which already copies Markdown files under its shared folder, puts them in place. The generator adds the folder to each parent's own agent (`agents.entries.<id>.memory.search.extraPaths`, never the global list); the agents find pages with `memory_search` and `memory_get`, keyword-only (`memory.search.provider: "none"`, already set). No agent gets a tool that writes to the folder, and shared agents and the mail readers keep memory search off. Not built: the memory-wiki plugin and its four tools, saving a page from a photo, manuals by link. The shared-folder part of T6 runs first, on an eval-only copy. No house-rules rule is needed.
caveats: Only Tony adds or changes a page, by typing or pasting it and deploying; that includes a page another planned card produces, such as the emergency page of CRT-13. A parent cannot save a page by text or by sending a photo.
Pages are found by their words when the agent searches; they are not in view at the start of a chat, and a scheduled text or a hand-off to a helper does not know them.

The folder is shared on purpose, which steps outside 'one data domain per person' by Tony's choice of 12 Oct. It holds household reference only: no copy of either parent's own notes, and by the default he kept, no child's health details.
The text of a page goes to the cloud model whenever a search returns it.
A date that needs a reminder does not belong here: it is a calendar event or a reminder.
The card rests on a search that has not been tried. If a sandboxed agent cannot find pages in a shared folder, the few facts go into the rendered family facts (F042) instead of a searched folder.
unverified: The shared-folder part of T6: that a search from a sandboxed parent's agent finds a page kept in a folder outside both workspaces, through a per-agent extra path. Not tried.

The installed code labels files indexed from outside an agent's workspace as untrusted origin (dist/memory-path-provenance-BiFQlpIk.mjs:32); whether that hides handbook pages or brings them back with a warning label was not tested.

That the same folder listed as an extra path on two agents is indexed for both and for no other agent: the multi-agent page describes a shared extra-path folder for reference material; not tried here.
That the deploy's existing copy step for shared Markdown files is a workable home for the pages: read in the deploy script, not tried with a handbook folder.
F043.safety: Shared between the two adults on purpose, for household reference only. No agent can write a page: only Tony does, through the reviewed deploy, so a planted instruction cannot be saved into it from a chat. The folder is added to the two parents' agents alone; shared agents and mail readers keep memory search off. No send path is added.

AUT-06.name: Teach Happy a routine (operator-reviewed skills), with a parent-run practice quiz as the first skill
AUT-06.description: A parent describes once how the family does something (party plan, ski-trip packing, school-form explainer); Tony turns it into a named skill, and after the next deploy Happy can load it when a later request fits the skill's one-line description. The first skill is a practice quiz that a parent runs from a study-guide photo, a pasted spelling list or a request for math facts: ten questions, one at a time, hint first, a running score and the answer key at the end.
AUT-06.example: 'Happy, learn our ski-trip packing routine: ask how many nights and who is coming, then list by person, and always include the kids' helmets.' Or Jordan sends a photo of the science study guide and texts: 'quiz us on this, 10 questions, one at a time.'
AUT-06.how:
Pipeline (AUT-06): Happy answers with the drafted procedure as plain text; Tony turns it into `skills//SKILL.md` in happy-config, reviews it, and happy-deploy copies it into that agent's workspace `skills/` folder. The model loads a skill by reading its SKILL.md, so `

-main` needs `read` in `tools.alsoAllow` and the sandbox tool allowlist; `skill_workshop` stays denied on every family agent. A routine of a few lines can live in AGENTS.md instead. Quiz (MKT-02): one such skill fixes the format (one question per message, one hint before revealing, a running score, the answer key at the end, no web lookups); a photo needs attachment intake (F002) and is read by the reply model's own vision; an optional one-shot reminder offers a re-quiz the night before.
depends_on: a skills step in happy-deploy and gen-family
automatic self-learning switched off in config (`skills.workshop.autonomous.mode: "off"`)
decision: who may request a new skill

`read` allowed on

-main in tools.alsoAllow and the sandbox tool allowlist (group:fs is denied today; per-person memory, F041, adds `write` and `edit` only, so `read` is a grant of its own)
F041's write-path hook refusing any write under skills/, proven with a test write (needed once F041 gives the same agent a read-write workspace)
F002 photo and PDF reading with inbound attachments switched on, for the quiz's photo route only

F007 automations tool on

-main, only for the optional re-quiz reminder
F003 voice over iMessage, its local spoken replies, only for reading spelling words aloud
caveats: Asking Happy to save a skill from iMessage does not work on this stack: sandboxed runs do not construct the `skill_workshop` tool, and the documented exception would publish with no pending draft and so skip Tony's review, which is one more reason to keep that tool off every family agent.
A skill is know-how: it cannot add tools or accounts, so 'learn to order the groceries' still ends at a list.

A skill is instruction text loaded into future sessions, so one written from a pasted web page or an email is a stored injection: author only from the parent's own words, and install no marketplace skills (an audit reported by The Hacker News found 341 malicious entries among 2,857 ClawHub skills in early 2026).

Turnaround is 'when Tony next deploys', and Happy does not run a skill every time: the prompt lists only each skill's name and one-line description, so that line has to be precise, and calling the skill by name (`/skill <name>`) is the sure route where that command is accepted from the sender.

The quiz is parent-run only: the kids are not users, the parent holds the phone and sends the answers, and a version a child uses alone waits for the kids agent (F072) and never uses a cloud model or cloud speech.

The ChatGPT or Gemini app on a parent's phone already makes a quiz from uploaded material, with hints and an end summary; Happy's only edge is that it lives in the same thread and can schedule the re-quiz.
Models write wrong answer keys, especially for arithmetic and for facts the sheet does not state, so tell it to quiz only from what is on the page and spot-check.

A text quiz shows spelling words on screen, so spelling practice needs the words read aloud with the local voice (F003), whose quality for spelling words is untried, and the running score lives in the conversation and is gone after the daily session reset.

Once per-person memory (F041) gives a parent's agent `write` and `edit` on a read-write workspace, the workspace skills folder sits inside what the agent can write: for that mode the docs describe a read-only copy only for bundled, managed and plugin skills (workspace-access.md:91) and do not say the workspace skills folder is protected. 'No model-written file reaches a skills folder' then rests on F041's in-house path hook, so that hook's proof must include a refused write to skills/.
AUT-06.safety: Operator review is the gate: `skill_workshop` stays denied on every family agent, a skill cannot widen tool policy, and no model-written file is meant to reach a skills folder. Once per-person memory (F041) lets the same agent write files in its workspace, that last point rests on F041's write-path hook and has to be proven with a refused write to skills/. The quiz is the riskier part: a photographed school worksheet is untrusted content, is not screened by the PDF privacy gate in F002, and goes to the cloud vision model under store:false. No child's account talks to a cloud model.
unverified: Whether a user-invocable skill command typed by an allowlisted non-owner iMessage sender is accepted on 2026.9.7.
That skill sync into the sandbox works with `workspaceAccess: "none"` (the docs say sandboxed runs read materialized copies).

That a `read`-only grant on a sandboxed

-main reaches the mirrored skills and nothing private; check at build time.

Whether a spoken reply arrives as a playable voice message or as a file in iMessage Basic mode.

G015.name: Read-only Gmail for each parent: a 07:00 weekday mail text and 'did I get an email about X?'
G015.description: Each parent approves read-only access to their own Gmail once, on Google's own screen; the token stays on the Mac mini, Happy never holds a password, and nothing in Gmail is changed, labelled, drafted or sent. Each weekday at 07:00 Eastern a locked-down mail reader texts its owner a short list of what needs a reply, has a deadline or involves money, with the school lines first and no links. A parent can also ask 'did I get an email about X?' and get the sender, the date and the gist from their own inbox.
G015.example: 07:00, text to Tony: 'Mail. School: a form for the third-grader is due back on Friday 16 October. Needs you: the plumber asks you to confirm Thursday's visit by tomorrow; a bill is due on Tuesday 20 October.' Later Jordan texts her own Happy 'did I get an email about class photo day?' and gets the sender, the date and one line of gist from her own inbox.
G015.how:
Connector: `gog mcp`, gog's own MCP server, as one host-side stdio entry under `mcp.servers` per parent, started with only that parent's token and narrowed with `--allow-tool` to the Gmail read tools; a read-only token each from `gog auth add` (`--services` Gmail only, `--gmail-scope readonly`). Reader: one generated `

-mail` agent per parent: `profile: "minimal"`, only `

-gmail__*` allowed (also in `tools.sandbox.tools`) and denied by name elsewhere, except on that parent's own agent once its lookup is on (see Lookup); memory search off; one cloud model, storage off, no fallback. Gate: the connector reaches Google and nothing else. The wave A runbook found that a firewall rule cannot name Google's hosts for this program, so it builds the gate as one firewall rule that blocks every direct connection by the connector plus a small local proxy that lets it reach three named Google hosts; Tony's yes to that is asked at the runbook's step A4. Text: one weekday 07:00 Eastern job per reader from the jobs script (G003), Gmail read tools only, delivered to its owner: own label, school lines first (F051), no links, medical mail by sender and subject only, silent on an empty morning. Lookup (Tony, 13 Oct): `

-main` hands a mail question to its own `

-mail` through `subagents.allowAgents`, with `subagents.requireAgentId: true` (the list governs only a call that names an agent; a call that names none would start a copy of the asking agent), with a two-minute default time limit. On 2026.9.7 an agent started by another keeps only the tools its asker is allowed (the asker's allowed tools and its denies are passed to the helper and applied last), so `

-main` is itself allowed the three `

-gmail` read tools (also in its sandbox tool list) and no longer denies that one server; its instructions tell it to hand every mail question to the reader and never to call those tools itself. The reader's own list, the three read tools and nothing else, is what narrows the hand-off. Eval-only copies of a parent's agent never hold a connector tool or the hand-off to a mail reader (except T5's throwaway pair in wave C, which reads only the test mailbox), so the lookup is tested live. House rules: adds the account-connector rule when that plugin is first created. From then the parent's own agent is blocked in code from calling the Gmail tools it holds, if test T5 shows that the check is told which agent is calling.
caveats: The read-only grant lets the connector read every message in the account. The school lines are picked out by the model, with no sender filter and no check, so it may miss a school mail or list one that is not; and mail that arrives during the day waits for the next morning's text.

Mail text goes to the cloud model on Tony's go-ahead of 12 Oct, and is read before the full firewall and the outbound proxy exist. Until OpenAI approves Zero Data Retention its abuse-monitoring log can keep that text for up to 30 days. Both points depart from the roadmap's rules for mail readers, by his choice.

Nothing about the connector has been tried on this Mac: gog is not installed, so its flags come from upstream docs, and whether a token from the published sign-in app outlives seven days on a personal account is test T1. If the day-8 search fails, the choice is a weekly sign-in per parent or a different connector.

'No links' and 'sender and subject only for medical mail' are instructions to the reader, not enforced limits. What limits harm is that the reader holds only Gmail read tools and its outputs are the scheduled text to its owner and, once the lookup is on, its answer to its owner's own agent.

The lookup goes two steps beyond the roadmap's mail design. Its answer comes back into the parent's own agent, which holds that parent's chats, can search the web and will later hand tasks to the web helper. And by Tony's decision of 13 Oct that agent is itself allowed the Gmail read tools, because a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed: an instruction, checked by a count of its tool calls, keeps it from reading mail itself, not a tool limit, until the house-rules plugin's check exists, and then only if test T5 allows that check. Only prompt rules and a seeded-mail test stand between them, so it goes live in its own step and can be switched off without touching the morning text.
Google's Gemini app already answers questions from a person's own Gmail and lists a daily digest among its scheduled actions; Happy adds only asking, and being told, in the iMessage thread.

With the lookup on, each mail question also leaves the reader's transcript of that hand-off on the Mac (archived an hour after it finishes and kept until the disk budget evicts it, unless the optional 30-day setting of the wave A runbook is switched on) and the answer in the parent's own chat transcript.
corrections: The 9 Oct needs list omits the sandbox-layer gate: with sandbox mode 'all', MCP tools stay hidden unless `tools.sandbox.tools` names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130). The minimal profile does not allow MCP tools implicitly either (same file, lines 36 and 41).

'Memory off' is not one switch in the installed docs: memory search has a per-agent override (`agents.entries.*.memory.search`, `enabled`, docs/reference/memory-config.md:31 and :102), dreaming is plugin-wide (docs/concepts/memory.md:275), and `excludeSessions.hookExternalContentSources` only matches hook sessions (docs/reference/memory-config.md:667).

'Send pinned to owner' only applies when the mail agent runs its own scheduled or hook turn: when spawned from `

-main` it always loses `message` and `session_status` (docs/tools/subagents/tool-policy.md:23), so its allow list must not consist of `session_status` alone.
The 9 Oct needs list puts `openclaw models status --agent --probe` in the deploy checks; the installed doc says a direct probe needs the Gateway stopped (docs/cli/models.md:121).

The 9 Oct verifier note says gogcli has no read-only-only Gmail scope. The upstream command reference lists `--gmail-scope full|readonly|send|read-send` and says `--readonly` on `gog auth add` requests read-only OAuth scopes, so a read-only grant can be requested; the catalog's hedge 'if the installed version supports it' can be firmed up, pending a check on the installed binary.

The 9 Oct text treats the `

-gmail` wrapper as new code. Upstream gogcli ships a stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`) that exposes only read tools unless `--allow-write` is passed, so the config entry can run gog directly with an `--allow-tool` list and no wrapper.

The 9 Oct needs list stops at the per-agent allow list. With sandbox mode 'all' (Happy's setting) the installed docs add a second gate: MCP tools are filtered out unless `tools.sandbox.tools` also names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130).

13 Oct, read in the installed code while the wave A runbook was written: an agent started through `sessions_spawn` keeps only the tools its asker is allowed. The spawn tool passes the asker's allow list and deny list to the child, also for a different target agent (dist/sessions-spawn-tool-B5tfhM3J.mjs:3244), and they are applied as the last filter, 'inherited tools' (dist/conversation-tool-policy-pipeline-D3eQnHfK.mjs:74); the docs say 'inherited tool policy' still applies (docs/tools/subagents/nesting.md:13). The lookup as first written, with the Gmail tools denied on the parent's own agent, could not have worked.

13 Oct: the card said no wrapper is needed for gog. The wave A runbook starts gog through a ten-line wrapper, which gives each sign-in its own keyring namespace and points gog at the local proxy; and it found that 2026.9.7 rejects a hand-off time limit set under one agent, so the limit is the gateway-wide default.

13 Oct: the wave A runbook builds each 07:00 text as two jobs, Tuesday to Friday looking back one day and Monday looking back three, because a scheduled message cannot carry the weekday; this page counts them as one text.

13 Oct, from the installed docs: `subagents.allowAgents` only governs a hand-off that names its target; one that names none starts a copy of the asking agent ('Default: only the requester agent', docs/tools/subagents/thread-bound-sessions.md:74), and `subagents.requireAgentId` is what refuses it. The lookup sets both.
unverified: gog is not installed on this Mac; its flags (`--gmail-scope readonly` and `--services` on `gog auth add`, `--allow-tool` on `gog mcp`) come from the upstream docs and must be confirmed with `gog mcp --list-tools` and `gog auth add --help` on the installed version.

T1: that publishing the self-made Google sign-in app to In production keeps a read-only Gmail token alive past seven days on a personal, unverified app. One search by hand on day 1 and again on day 8 or later, before the rest is built on the token; Google's scope page marks gmail.readonly as a Restricted scope.

Whether each adult's token can sit in a folder of its own under the happy user: upstream says tokens use the platform keyring by default with a file backend for headless hosts; splitting them with a per-adult GOG_HOME is an inference from the paths doc. The wave A runbook read upstream's source: a separate folder does not separate keyring entries, so it keeps each sign-in in happy's login Keychain under a namespace of its own and starts gog through a short wrapper; Tony's yes to both is asked at its step A4.

T2: that the minimal tool profile plus a per-agent allow shows each reader exactly one account server and shows it to no other agent (except that parent's own agent once its lookup is on, which is allowed the three tools on purpose); the roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed on this version. The 'read the other parent's mail' canary is run both ways.

T5, the connector turn: whether a plugin's blocking check is called for connector tools at all and, since 13 Oct, whether it is told which agent is calling, for a parent's own agent and for a helper it started. The docs say 'every tool call in the run' (plugins/hooks/tool-policy.md:222) but no sentence names MCP tools. It decides whether the account-connector rule can be written when the house-rules plugin is first created.

Whether a parent's own agent can see or quote the 07:00 text when the parent replies to it: checked at go-live. If it can, mail text reaches that agent even with the lookup switched off, and Tony signs that as the same departure from the roadmap as the lookup.

For the lookup, T4: that a hand-off from the parent's agent to its own mail reader returns the answer in the same chat while agents cannot see each other's sessions; and that a reader started this way keeps its three Gmail tools, which is read from the installed code and has not been run.

For the lookup, the seeded mail: a planted mail that tells the reader to make the parent's agent search for, save or pass on something must cause no tool call on the parent's agent in three runs (the planted mail also asks that agent to search the mailbox itself, which it is allowed to do and told not to), and the other parent's agent must be refused the reader. If either lookup test fails, the lookup stays off and the morning text is unaffected.

Whether this OpenAI account will be approved for Zero Data Retention; until then the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to mail text sent to the model. The per-person provider setting that sends store false was verified in M1 and not re-read here.

That a parent's own agent, allowed the Gmail read tools for the hand-off, keeps to its instruction and never calls them itself: a behaviour, checked by its tool-call record at go-live and at the exit test, and not enforced until the house-rules plugin's check exists, and then only if test T5 allows that check.
G015.safety: Each reader holds private mail and reads outsiders' text, so it has no way out: only Gmail read tools, and two outputs: the scheduled text, which the jobs script addresses from the family file, and, once the lookup is on, its answer to its owner's own agent. One reader, connector and token per parent; the two parents are held apart by tool permissions, an explicit deny and two tests until the house-rules plugin exists. The lookup is the weaker half: once it is on, the parent's own agent is allowed the same three read tools so that the reader it starts can use them, and only its instructions and a count of its tool calls keep it from reading mail itself.

F049.name: Email me this: a long answer sent to the asker's own inbox
F049.description: A parent texts 'email me this' and the long answer, table or plan lands in that parent's own inbox as plain text; either parent can ask. It is sent from the Gmail address Happy already has unless Tony names another. The only address the send tool accepts is the asker's own: a check in code blocks every other send, and blocks when the check itself fails.
F049.example: Jordan texts: 'Email me that comparison.' The full text arrives in her own inbox as plain text from Happy's address. A send that names anyone else on the To, cc or bcc line, or that goes out as a reply-all, is blocked.
F049.how: One shared mail-out server on the host: gog run as an MCP server for the sending address with its write and Gmail-send flags and only `gmail_send_message` registered, signed in with a send-only grant if the installed gog offers one. It is allowed by name on each parent's own agent, denied on the mail readers and every shared agent, and sits behind the same gate as the mail readers' connector (wave A's blocking rule and the local proxy's Google hosts). The card adds one rule to the house-rules plugin, the send-to-owner rule: a send is blocked unless the caller is a parent's own agent and the one recipient is that agent's owner, read from the family file, with no cc, bcc, reply or reply-all target, send-as alias or HTML body. The check fails closed. Before go-live: T5's send-tool turn, then the roadmap's five seeded ways to change the recipient (the other parent and a reply-all among them) and an injected web page. No send cap.
caveats: The promise that nobody else can be a recipient rests on one in-house rule, and it is not yet shown that the check sees every field that can set a recipient: to, cc and bcc, and also the reply fields, because the upstream page for the mail tool says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target'. The seeded sends, a reply-all among them, must all be blocked before this goes live.
The check blocks a wrong recipient; it does not correct it, because the docs describe rewriting parameters for host-owned tools only.
Plain text only: a table arrives as lined-up text, not as a formatted table. A long iMessage already delivers the same text; what this adds is the answer filed in the inbox.

Pinning the recipient does not close every way out: the mailed text is often built from research results, and a link in it can carry private text in its address to whoever runs that site once it is clicked. A link is only as trustworthy as the result it came from.
No send cap: a runaway loop could fill the asker's own inbox until someone notices or the agent's spend cap stops it.
Signing Happy's existing Google account in on the Mac mini for sending is a new use of that account. A send-only grant keeps the token from reading that mailbox, if the installed gog supports it.
unverified: That the blocking check is called for the mail-out server's send tool and is given every field that can set a recipient: the upstream page names recipients, reply context, a reply-all target and send-as aliases as inputs but does not list the tool's input schema, so whether cc and bcc are separate fields is not known (T5's send-tool turn, then the five-way test).
That the check is told which agent is calling, so it can look up that agent's owner; the rule refuses the send when the agent id or the owner lookup is missing (T5).
That the installed gog offers a send-only grant (`gog auth add --gmail-scope send` was read in the upstream command reference) and that the MCP send tool works under it.
That gog's MCP write, Gmail-send and tool-filter flags behave as documented on the installed version; the roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed.
F049.safety: Each parent's own agent holds private data and reads outside content, so its mail way out is pinned in code: the house-rules plugin blocks any send not addressed to the calling agent's owner alone, and blocks when the check fails. No mail reader or shared agent gets the tool. Plain text only, so no remote image can report back.
