CRT-05.name: Half page for Jordan: how to tell that Happy is down
CRT-05.description: Jordan gets one printed half page: how to recognise that Happy is down, that nothing in the house is broken, and who to call. After a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, as the roadmap row he chose says. There is no envelope, no password on paper and no Terminal step.
CRT-05.example: A power cut while Tony is out. Happy stops answering, and Jordan reads the half page: no reply within a few minutes means Happy is down, nothing is broken, and it comes back when Tony unlocks the Mac.
CRT-05.how: No software, so no house-rules rule. Tony writes and prints a half page for Jordan: (1) how to tell that Happy is down: no reply within a few minutes, or the error line a parent sees when a turn fails, worded from what test T8 showed on his own phone; (2) nothing is broken: after a power cut the Mac waits at the disk-unlock screen and Happy stays down until Tony unlocks it; (3) who to call. Not on the page and not built: an envelope, a password, Terminal commands, a pause phrase, an alert to her phone and the Legacy Contact step. The house scripts stay Tony-only.
depends_on: T8 run first (it belongs with the printed stop-and-check sheet, G005): Tony has seen on his own phone what a failed turn looks like, so the page is worded from that
Tony provides the 'who to call' line at execution
caveats: With the half page alone Jordan cannot bring Happy back: after a power cut Happy stays down until Tony unlocks the Mac at home, which is what the roadmap row he chose says.
A small UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the disk-unlock screen.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.
The page has no pause step: Jordan has no stop phrase of her own and is not a command owner.
Jordan gets no 'Happy is down' alert. She learns of an outage when she texts Happy and gets no answer.

An envelope so that she could restart Happy is not part of this card. If Tony ever wants one, his own unlock test (T10) comes first and it holds at most the happy user's password; an administrator credential on paper for anyone but Tony is a separate decision that has not been taken.
CRT-05.safety: Nothing is granted to any agent, and the page holds no credential and no command. No secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's alone.
unverified: What a parent sees on iMessage when a turn fails: read from the docs and the code, not tried (T8).

MAC-04.name: Paired-device deny list, deployed before the first device is paired
MAC-04.description: Just before the first device is paired (Tony's iPhone in OCL-01 or the virtual Mac of the screen-control pilot, MAC-02, whichever comes first), a short list in the Gateway config says which commands no paired phone or Mac may run: reading a phone's location, contacts, calendar, reminders, photos and motion, and driving, viewing or running commands on a Mac. The family sees no change; the pilot later lifts two entries for its own runs.
MAC-04.example: On the day his phone is paired Tony deploys the list, checks that the mail connector still works, and only then makes the setup code.
MAC-04.how: Config only, with no house-rules rule, written on the day the first device is paired, from the installed version's docs. `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` gets `computer.act`; the desktop host commands (`system.run`, `system.run.prepare`, `system.which`, `browser.proxy`, `browser.proxy.upload.v1`, `mcp.tools.call.v1`, `screen.snapshot`, `desktop.stream`); the iPhone data commands (`location.get`, `contacts.search`, `calendar.events`, `reminders.list`, `photos.latest`, `motion.activity`, `motion.pedometer`); and the four `talk.ptt.*` commands until Talk is set up. Nothing is added to `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`; `gateway.nodes.pluginTools.enabled: false`; pairing stays manual (`autoApproveLocal` and `sshVerify` false, `autoApproveCidrs` unset), and a Mac is never paired with a setup link. Deploy, confirm that the mail connector and any browser still work, and only then make a phone's setup code. After pairing, read the device's declared commands and deny any unwanted one by its exact name. happy-inspect's posture check gains the deny list, `sshVerify` and `pluginTools.enabled`. One rule, no code: never enable `cua-computer` on the Mac mini.
depends_on: No other card: an ordinary deploy, done on the day the first device is paired and before any setup code is made
caveats: Until that day nothing in config covers a device paired by mistake: with a setup code, a phone's default data reads would be live at once. The written rule meanwhile is no Mac app, no pairing and no setup code; the one documented line for screen control, `computer.act`, can ride along in any earlier deploy.

A setup code approves a device and its first command list in one step, so the list has to be deployed before the code is made, not after. For a Mac no setup link is used, so the device and then its command list are approved by hand in two steps.
The list is Gateway-wide, not per device: a pilot that lifts an entry lifts it for every paired device.

The list does not empty a device's commands. OpenClaw's defaults still allow `camera.list`, `device.info`, `device.status` and `system.notify` on an iPhone, so the phone's declared commands are read at pairing and any unwanted one is added.
If the check shows that the mail connector or a browser broke, `browser.proxy` and `mcp.tools.call.v1` come off the list while no Mac is paired and go back before any Mac is.
The `cua-computer` rule is a second lock: on macOS that route also needs the OpenClaw Mac app, which is not installed on the Mac mini, so no check code is written for it.
MAC-04.safety: Pure tightening: a limit in config that a prompt cannot change. Until the screen-control pilot no agent holds the `computer` tool, and none holds the nodes tools (each parent's agent denies `group:nodes` and the inbox agent has no tools), so a paired device gives agents nothing new.
unverified: That deny entries for `system.run` and the other host commands apply exactly as for `computer.act`; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.
That denying `browser.proxy` and `mcp.tools.call.v1` for paired devices leaves the connectors and any browser on the Gateway itself untouched; checked on the day, when the mail connector exists.

Which command name sits behind the iPhone app's 'Screen snapshot' capability: the docs list `screen.snapshot` as a desktop command and do not name the phone's, so it is read from the phone at pairing and denied by its exact name.

MAC-02.name: Screen-control pilot on a clean, throwaway virtual Mac (attended by Tony)
MAC-02.description: An experimental pilot: Happy controls the screen of a clean, throwaway virtual Mac that holds no Apple Account, Messages or saved passwords, never Happy's own desktop. It starts with one 'step zero' test and ends there if that fails. If it passes, Tony starts and watches every run of one chore he names at execution; nobody starts a run by text.
MAC-02.example: Step zero: in the throwaway virtual Mac, one screenshot is taken and one click is made on an empty desktop while Tony watches. Later Tony starts the chore he named, watches it and reads the result: 'done' or 'stopped: a sign-in window appeared'.
MAC-02.how: Step zero first; if it fails the pilot ends, and no real desktop is ever used. A throwaway macOS guest on the Mac mini (for example with the Lume CLI); OpenClaw.app installed in it and paired by hand as its own device, with no setup link; proof that the app runs there without operator rights; then, with the MAC-04 entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` lifted, one screenshot and one click invoked by Tony as operator. If it passes: one `desk` agent with memory off, its own capped model key, the minimal tool profile and only `computer` (in its tool allow and in `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`); the guest may reach only the gateway and is reset before every run. Tony starts and watches each run, and stops it with 'Allow Computer Control' in the guest's app or by putting the deny entries back. Test: his chore, run a few times, once with a planted instruction on screen. House-rules plugin: no rule while only Tony starts runs.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny list in place first; its entries for `computer.act` and `screen.snapshot` are lifted for the pilot. The list is Gateway-wide, so no other Mac is paired meanwhile, and if a phone is paired by then its approved command list is re-read first
Tony provides the chore at execution: one family chore that no app or script already handles, with nothing from the never list in it (no payment, purchase, booking, lock or CAPTCHA)
Step zero passes; if it does not, the pilot ends there
Disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest (OpenClaw's virtual-Mac page asks for about 60 GB of free disk)

A route from the guest to the gateway, which listens on the Mac mini only: the guest's own tailnet identity or an SSH tunnel, limited to the gateway's address and reviewed as a change to the M0 baseline
Tony provides a new capped model key for the desk agent at execution, created by hand (each agent has its own key)
caveats: The guest is not empty of secrets: the app inside it is signed in to the family gateway. Until step zero shows it running as a device with no operator rights, the agent driving the screen could open a console to everything the clean desk was built to keep away.
Pairing the Mac app pairs a whole device: shell commands, a browser proxy, connector calls and a desktop stream arrive with pointer control. Those stay on the deny list.
There is no check per click and no approval per action: dozens of clicks run unreviewed, so Tony watches every run, and nothing sent by text stops a run in mid-task.

Red-team research on computer-use agents reports injected on-screen instructions succeeding in a large share of attempts, so the tool's built-in warning to the model is a tripwire, not a control. What exists on the controlled desktop is the real boundary.
A desktop that is never reset is the agent's memory: files, open windows and the clipboard carry over from one run to the next.
A pass shows that the chore can be done, not that screen control is safe. Letting anyone start a run by text would need a stop check in code first, as a rule in the house-rules plugin.
MAC-02.safety: The desk agent reads untrusted content (the screen) and holds no memory, accounts or message tool. Its limits are config a prompt cannot change: `computer` on that agent alone, every other device command on the deny list, a guest that reaches only the gateway and is reset before each run, with the app's operator access proven absent first. Never Happy's own desktop; nothing from the never list.
unverified: That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its macOS permissions, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest with a virtual display. Step zero settles it.
Whether the Mac app can run in the guest as a device with no operator rights. Step zero settles it.
How to restrict a Lume guest's network to one host address.

That with `cua-computer` never enabled on the Mac mini, a `computer` call with no target lands on the guest and never on Happy's own desktop; the docs say the sole connected computer is used, and it was not run.

How Tony invokes one screenshot and one click as operator in step zero, and later starts a run on the desk agent and reads its result; the docs say an operator with write access can invoke a paired device's command, and none of this was tried.
Apple's licence for the installed macOS 27 (the macOS 26 licence, read in an earlier run, allows up to two additional macOS instances in virtual machines for personal use).
The guest's memory cost; OpenClaw's page states disk only.

OCL-01.name: OpenClaw app on Tony's iPhone: chat with files, then Talk mode (Tony only)
OCL-01.description: Tony can also reach Happy in the free OpenClaw iPhone app, on his phone only: a chat that is documented to take photos, PDFs and other files (not yet tried here), with a share sheet and an offline queue, and, as a second and experimental step, Talk mode, a spoken back-and-forth with his own agent. Tapping approvals in the app and its Talk settings pages need Full access; with Limited access those stay in iMessage and the Control UI. It is a first paired device, and not the connected idle iPhone Tony once described.
OCL-01.example: Tony attaches a PDF in the app with + -> File and asks 'what do I have to sign, and by when?'. With Talk set up, he asks aloud what the weather is tomorrow and hears the answer.
OCL-01.how: 1. Two checks on the Control UI already on Tony's phone: does a pending approval raise a lock-screen alert (Web Push), and can tony-main read one harmless uploaded PDF. They show what the app adds. 2. MAC-04 is deployed. 3. Tony says Full or Limited; the App Store app is paired with a setup code from the Control UI or `openclaw qr` (`--limited` for Limited) over the Tailscale Serve URL. One code issues a device session and an operator session, so the phone's declared commands are read afterwards and unwanted ones denied by name. No agent gets the nodes tools. Revoking a lost phone is one line on the printed sheet (G005). 4. Talk, experimental: take the four `talk.ptt.*` commands off the deny list, set `talk.provider`, leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off, and set `talk.agentId` to a memory-less agent. Talk runs on the chat open in the app, normally tony-main. Not built: realtime voice, a second phone, an upload gate. House-rules plugin: no rule.
depends_on: MAC-04 deny list deployed before the setup code is made (iPhone data commands and push-to-talk denied, tools published by devices off)

F002 photos and PDFs live first: its planted-file test has passed and the instruction line that says Happy cannot see files is replaced. A file sent from the app comes in through the Gateway's own upload path, not the iMessage switch, and that path is tried here for the first time
The OpenClaw iOS app from the App Store on Tony's iPhone; Tailscale is already on the phone for the Control UI
Tony provides at execution: Full or Limited access for his phone (tap approvals in the app and its Talk settings pages need Full; the Control UI on the phone keeps admin either way)
The revoke step for a lost phone (`openclaw devices revoke`), which the printed sheet (G005) carries

For Talk: a speech provider under `talk.provider` (the built-in Mac voice set up for spoken replies in F003, if it passes Talk's check, which is untested), or the iPhone's own system voice as the fallback
caveats: The app is a chat client, an operator console for the whole Gateway and a paired device at once. Limited access drops only the admin scope and keeps Gateway-wide write, read and approvals scopes; since Tony's phone already holds two Control UI entries with admin, what is new is the device role and the hosted push relay.
Tony's phone only: operator access is not a boundary between people, so a paired phone can read both parents' sessions.
Limited access does not deliver tap approvals in general or the Talk settings pages, and a file upload from the app or the Control UI has never been tried.

App Store builds receive push through OpenClaw's hosted relay, a service outside the tailnet, and iOS suspends the app in the background, so device commands need the app in front and voice is best-effort.

Talk: Apple's speech recognition on iOS may use network services, so audio can leave the house, and the transcript goes to the cloud model like any typed message. Nothing identifies the speaker: whoever talks near the phone is taken to be Tony, so a child must not use Talk.

iMessage with photo and PDF reading (F002) and the Control UI already on the phone cover most of this; the app adds the share sheet, the offline queue, the native approval inbox (Full access only) and Talk.

Device commands are denied in the Gateway config before pairing (MAC-04) and no agent holds the nodes tools, so the phone gives agents no new tool or data. Files reach Tony's own agent as outside content, like iMessage attachments. Talk runs on his own agent with its tools and memory. Never for a child.

F020.name: Research helper extra readers: a read-only browser for pages that need JavaScript, and text from videos and podcasts
F020.description: The research helper (F019) can also read public pages that show nothing without JavaScript, logged out, and pull the text out of videos that have captions and podcasts that publish a transcript, so a parent can ask for the main points from a link. The browser is kept read-only in code: no clicking, typing, form filling or uploads. Bot walls and logins stop it.
F020.example: A parent texts a link to a public page that shows nothing without JavaScript and asks what it says about sign-up dates; the helper opens it in the logged-out browser and the parent's own agent relays the dates with the link. Or Tony texts a link to a long video that has captions and asks for the main points.
F020.how: Used by the research helper (F019) only; allowed on each parent's agent as well, for the hand-off. (1) Browser: the `browser` tool in the roadmap's sandbox browser container, on its own network with the home network blocked; `sandbox.browser.enabled` for the helper only, `allowHostControl` left false, `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`, the tool named in the helper's tool allow and sandbox tool allow lists. Under the 13 Oct pattern a helper keeps only the tools its asker is allowed, so the browser tool has to be allowed on each parent's agent as well for the hand-off to carry it; whether that also needs the sandbox browser switched on for the parent's agent is not known and is settled in this wave's plan. The image is built from a source checkout; if it cannot be built, the browser half is not built, and no host browser is used. (2) House-rules plugin, one rule: for the helper, a short allowlist of read-only browser action names (status, tabs, open, navigate, focus, close, snapshot, text, screenshot); everything else, `act` and `upload` included, is blocked, failing closed. (3) Video and podcast text: a small connector on the Mac mini, allowed to the helper and, so that a hand-off can carry it, to each parent's agent (which is told never to call it itself), and denied by name elsewhere, wraps `summarize --extract --json` with `--firecrawl off`, no keys and no transcription fallback, and refuses home-network addresses itself. Planted-page cases join the eval suite.
caveats: Bot walls, logins, CAPTCHAs and two-factor prompts stop it. They are reported, never solved, and the docs say sandboxed browser sessions are more likely to be flagged as bots.

The browser image cannot be built from the npm install; it needs a source checkout. There is no fallback to a browser on the Mac itself: if the image cannot be built, only the video and podcast reader ships.

Read-only means no clicking, typing or scrolling, so a page that shows its content only after a click or a scroll stays unreadable. Allowing scrolling or hovering back later needs a further check written then, with an eval case each.
The action names come from the installed 2026.9.7 browser tool and can change with any update. Blocking by default keeps a new action blocked, but the rule needs its test after every OpenClaw update.

The video and podcast reader runs on the Mac mini outside the address checks that cover the page reader and the browser, and it has third-party extraction fallbacks of its own; the wrapper has to switch those off and check the address itself.
A video without captions or a podcast without a published transcript returns nothing: no transcription is set up.
corrections: The catalog says to 'use the host profile'; because research must stay sandboxed, the browser tool defaults to the sandbox browser, and the host profile needs `agents.defaults.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` plus an explicit host target.

The catalog's install line names the tap formula steipete/tap/summarize (as the bundled skill does); the upstream README opened in this run gives `npm install --global @steipete/summarize` or `brew install summarize`.
unverified: How often the pages a parent cares about block a headless, logged-out browser; not measured.

Whether the blocking check sees the browser call's action name, and whether it is given the helper's own id when the helper runs as a hand-off (T5; the names were read from the tool's schema, not seen in a live call).
Whether script-rendered pages can be read with no waiting, clicking or scrolling.

Whether the sandbox browser gives the helper a working `browser` tool with the top-level `browser.enabled` left false; the sandbox page says it is not required, the browser setup page says the tool needs it.
With open and navigate allowed, whether a link straight to a file is saved into the browser's downloads folder without the download action being called.

What `summarize` returns for a video without captions when no transcription is configured, and which of its flags exist in the installed version (`--youtube auto` appears in the bundled skill; check `summarize --help` after install).
Whether `summarize` can be made to send its calls through the outbound proxy; if not, its firewall rule and the wrapper's own address check are its only limits.
Whether a parent's agent can be allowed the `browser` tool for the hand-off's sake without the sandbox browser being switched on for that agent too: not read anywhere and not tried.
F020.safety: The helper holds no private data, memory or accounts, and its browser never holds a login. Each parent's agent is allowed the same tools only so that the hand-off can carry them; the coded rule keeps that agent from using them itself (for the video reader only if wave C's T5 allowed the connector rule; otherwise an instruction and its tool-call record do). Only read-only browser actions pass, in code that fails closed; page scripts are off and the home network is out of reach, so bookings and CAPTCHA boxes stay out of reach. A task handed to it may carry the town and ages, never names or the school.

F076.name: Lights and speakers by text: Hue and Sonos through a memory-less home agent, with a read-only 'still on' check
F076.description: A parent texts Happy to switch Hue rooms and scenes by name, or to play a Sonos favourite, pause the music or set a room's volume, under one hard volume cap enforced in code. Separately, at an evening time Tony sets, he gets a text only if lights or speakers are still on; that check switches nothing. Locks, garage, alarm and gate are never included.
F076.example: A parent texts: 'Downstairs lights off and pause the music.' At the time Tony set, and only if something is on, he gets a text that starts with the job's label and names the lights and the speaker that are still on.
F076.how: Step 1, read-only: a no-model job from the jobs script runs the `openhue` and `sonos` status commands on the Mac mini at the evening time Tony names and texts him only if something is on (`NO_REPLY` otherwise). Step 2, switching: a sandboxed `home` agent with no memory, no web tool and no message tool, on its own capped model key, reached by hand-off from each parent's agent, holds in-house tools that wrap the two command-line programs. Under the 13 Oct pattern each parent's agent is allowed the same tools, so that the hand-off can carry them, and is told to hand every command to the home agent. Hue: rooms and scenes by name, the bridge key kept in `~/.openhue/config.yaml`. Sonos: favourites, pause and volume, with one hard volume cap in the tool's code (Tony's number); no play-by-search. No quiet hours and no night cap; a room Tony wants left out is left out in the tool's code. The gateway's node process needs the macOS Local Network permission, or `--ip` per speaker. House-rules plugin: one rule, that only the home agent may call these tools (T5 decides whether it can be written); the cap sits inside the Sonos tool. Not built: Home Assistant, the TV, announcements.
caveats: This switches things in the house, so the volume cap is in the tool's code and not in the prompt. The number is Tony's starting value, not a sourced one.
Neither command-line tool is installed, and the bridge and the two speakers come from the 9 Oct scan and were not re-checked.
Favourites only: play-by-search is left out, because auto-playing the first search hit has no content filter.

Every command is two model turns, because the parent's agent hands it to the home agent. Each parent's agent is allowed the tools only so that the hand-off can carry them (Tony, 13 Oct); letting it call them itself would be one turn and is not done.
No quiet hours and no night cap: a parent's own late command is carried out. The Hue app can already switch lights at a set time, so the evening text is a nudge, not the switching.
Home Assistant, TV control and spoken announcements are not built.
corrections: 'sonoscli is go install only' is wrong: the project's install page recommends Homebrew (a steipete tap) and also offers prebuilt release archives; go install needs Go 1.26 or later. Only the bundled skill's metadata is limited to go install, so Go does not have to be installed on the Mac mini.

'Isolated runs cannot approve' is too strong: the exec approvals doc says approvals from scheduled runs are delivered to connected approval clients (Control UI, the apps) and the run waits, but they never go to chat channels and are denied at once when no such client is connected. For an iMessage-only household the conclusion is unchanged: use a dry-run period, not per-call approval.
unverified: Philips Hue's own local API documentation sits behind a developer login and was not opened; only the OpenHue CLI pages were.
Whether the gateway needs the Local Network permission for plain HTTPS to the bridge; the bundled skills document it only for Sonos discovery.
That the two programs report 'on' states in a form a short script can parse reliably; neither is installed.
That a hand-off to the home agent returns its result to the parent's agent (T4, first tried with the research helper, F019).
That a no-model job run by Happy's scheduler can reach the bridge and the speakers on the home network once the firewall blocks programs by default.
That the house-rules check is told which agent calls an in-house tool, so that a parent's own agent can be blocked from the tools it only holds for the home agent (T5).
F076.safety: The home agent can change lights and speakers, so it holds no memory, family data, web tool or message tool, and is reached only by a bounded hand-off. Each parent's agent, which reads outside content, is allowed the same tools for the hand-off's sake; the house-rules rule, or an instruction alone if that rule cannot be written, keeps it from switching anything itself. Its tools' code offers only named rooms and scenes, favourites, pause and volume under a hard cap, and has no command for locks, garage, alarm or gate. The evening check runs no model and switches nothing.

F080.name: Printing: 'print this' for an attached PDF or photo, and pages Happy wrote
F080.description: A parent texts 'print this' with an attached PDF or photo and it prints on the printer at home, with a cap on copies; Happy can also print a page it has just written at the parent's request, such as the emergency card. This matters mainly when the parent is away from home, since a phone on the home Wi-Fi may already print by itself. Links and ordinary web pages are not printed, and nothing prints by itself.
F080.example: Tony, still at work, texts a form as a PDF with 'print this, one copy', so it is on the printer when he gets home.
F080.how: First the thirty-second check: from an iPhone on the home Wi-Fi, open any PDF, tap Share and then Print, and see whether the printer Tony names appears. Then one print queue is added once on the Mac mini with `lpadmin`. One in-house tool on each parent's own agent calls `lp -d <queue> -n <copies>` on the Mac mini, with the queue fixed and a copies cap in the tool's code. It prints two things only: a PDF or photo the parent attached in that chat (photo and PDF reading, F002, must be on), and a page of plain text Happy wrote in that chat because the parent asked, such as the emergency card (CRT-13). No link is fetched: a parent who has a link saves the file on the phone and attaches it. Nothing prints on a schedule. House-rules plugin: no rule; both limits are inside the tool. One planted-file case joins the eval suite.
caveats: The printer is known only from a network scan and is unconfirmed; that it is a large-format photo printer rests on a web search summary, because the maker's page refused a direct fetch.
If the thirty-second check shows that a phone on the home Wi-Fi can already print, Happy's gain is printing while away from home and printing pages it wrote.
The print queue has not been added, and a driverless queue for this printer has not been tried.
Attached files only: no links and no web pages. Printing or saving a web page stays a two-tap job on the phone.
No page prints by itself on Sunday and there are no chore turns: no chore rota is on record. A parent who wants paper asks Happy to print the week once calendar questions (F009) exist.
A print job cannot be recalled once it is sent.
unverified: Whether a driverless queue created with `lpadmin` works with the printer Tony names; no queue was created.
Whether the printer supports printing from the phones; no first-party page could be opened, so the thirty-second check settles it.
How the print tool gets at a file a parent attached: whether an in-house tool is given the attachment's path on the Mac mini was not tried.
Whether the firewall, once it blocks every program by default, needs a rule for the Mac's print system to reach the printer.
F080.safety: Printing goes to one fixed queue with a copies cap in the tool's code, and only on a parent's own request. With no link fetch, the agent that holds a parent's notes gains no new way to reach an outside address: the only way out added is paper at home. No scheduled job gets the tool.

AUT-01.description: Tony hands Happy a project with an end date; Happy keeps one project note among his saved notes, and a recurring reminder texts him every few days to check in. When he replies, Happy lists what is still open from the note, and he cancels the reminder when the project is done. It works for Tony only: Jordan's agent cannot create timed jobs.
AUT-01.example: Tony texts: 'Help me plan the garage clean-out by the end of the month, and check in with me every few days.' Every third day he gets 'Garage clean-out: reply status for what is open'; he replies 'status' and Happy lists the open items from the note.
AUT-01.how: No new mechanism, on Tony's agent only. (1) The project note is one of his saved notes (F041): the goal, the end date, decisions and open items. It records only what he typed or confirmed. (2) One ordinary recurring reminder (F007) at a fixed gap, for example every three days, whose text asks him to reply 'status'. It carries no tools, so it cannot read the note. (3) One rule in the agent's instructions: keep the note current, and on 'status' list the open items from it. Tony cancels the reminder when the project is done. A lookup he asks for in chat goes to the research helper (F019). House-rules plugin: no new rule; the reminder passes the rule F007 adds (a text to the asker only, no web address, no tools). Not built: a job that sets its own gap, reads the note or removes itself.
depends_on: F041 saved notes (the project note is one of them)
F007 timed reminders, with its reminder rule in the house-rules plugin (Tony's agent only)
F019 research helper, only for lookups Tony asks for in chat
Tony provides at execution: a first project to try it on, and how often the check-in should come
caveats: Tony only: Jordan's agent cannot create timed jobs, because she is not a command owner.
The check-in text does not list the open items by itself; Tony replies to get them. Happy does not vary the gap, and the reminder is not removed at the end date: he cancels it.
The conversation resets every morning at 04:00, so the project note is the only continuity between days.
The note holds only what Tony typed or confirmed. What a web lookup found stays in the chat until he says what to keep.
No bookings, purchases or invitations are sent: the output is options, links and drafts. A static checklist is still easier in a shared Notes or Reminders list; Happy adds the nudge and the lookups.
AUT-01.safety: No new tool, grant or way out. The note is one of Tony's own saved notes, and the nudge is an ordinary reminder that passes the reminder rule in the house-rules plugin: a text to the asker only, no web address, no tools. Web lookups stay with the memory-less research helper (F019). Nothing on the never list is reachable.
unverified: That a recurring reminder at a fixed gap of days can be created from an iMessage turn under F007's rule (T7 covers creating a reminder at all).
That one note per project is found again by keyword after the 04:00 reset (T6 covers saving and finding a note in general).

sources.title: System prompt: long-running-work guidance
sources.supports: OpenClaw's built-in guidance tells an agent to handle future follow-up, such as checking back later and recurring work, with scheduled jobs; together with the vendor's advice to keep a longer aim in a project note with a review date (already on the item) this is the feature's pattern.

adds: From AUT-03 (Self-paced watch loop (/loop and paced automations)): The /loop command runs on the same scheduling tool and needs the same prerequisites as AUT-01's check-ins: the delivery pin extended to automations add and update with webhooks refused, cron.triggers.enabled false, and owner status. If that grant is ever made, /loop works for an owner too; house rule is an explicit interval of 15 minutes or more and a stop condition, and since it sees only search snippets, page watching stays with F029. The round-1 review of OCL-06 takes /loop out of that entry, so this note is where /loop is described.
review_notes: All nine sources check out, but the safety case has a hole: the `automations` tool this feature depends on can set a job's delivery to any chat or to a webhook URL, and command-owner status lets either parent's agent read and edit the other's jobs. The project note also collides with the F041 rule that tainted turns cannot write memory. Value lowered to 3.

removed.name: Drive the spare iPhone through iPhone Mirroring and the computer tool
removed.reason: Driving a spare iPhone through iPhone Mirroring means letting an agent control Happy's whole Mac desktop, right next to Messages, and the phone would have to share Happy's Apple Account.

sources.title: iPhone Mirroring: Use your iPhone from your Mac (Apple Support)

removed.name: Green-bubble SMS through the spare iPhone
removed.reason: A SIM in a spare iPhone for ordinary text messages costs a monthly line, puts a second device on Happy's Apple Account and serves nobody, since both parents use iMessage and the school texts their own numbers.

sources.title: Forward text messages from your iPhone to other devices (Apple Support)
sources.supports: An iPhone can let a Mac signed in to the same Apple Account send and receive its text messages, as long as the iPhone is on and connected.

sources.title: iMessage media and targets

sources.title: SMS

sources.title: Node device commands

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
sources.supports: NIST classes codes sent over the phone network (SMS or voice) as a restricted authenticator.

removed.name: Developer automation over USB (XCUITest, WebDriverAgent, Appium)
removed.reason: Developer automation over a cable can tap any app, but it needs Xcode, Developer Mode, weekly re-signing and an agent holding everything at once; it is a testing tool, not a family feature.

sources.title: Device Preparation (Appium XCUITest Driver docs)
sources.supports: A real iPhone must be trusted by the Mac and have Developer Mode and Enable UI Automation switched on before Appium can drive it.

sources.title: Provisioning Profile (Appium XCUITest Driver docs)
sources.supports: WebDriverAgent has to be signed with a development team and a valid provisioning profile before it installs on a real device.

sources.title: Enabling Developer Mode on a device (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.anchor: reduces the security of your device
sources.supports: Turning on Developer Mode shows an alert that it lowers the device's security and requires a restart and passcode.

sources.title: Developer account overview (Apple Developer)
sources.supports: With a free Apple Account, registered devices and provisioning profiles for on-device installs expire after 7 days.

sources.title: XCUIAutomation (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.supports: Apple presents its UI automation framework as a way to test that your own app's interface works.

removed.name: Rejected: reading 2FA codes, banking apps, an unlocked unattended phone
removed.reason: Reading two-factor codes, opening banking apps and leaving a phone unlocked and unattended stay on the never list, with the text-message commands denied in config.

sources.title: Node command policy

sources.title: Node device commands
sources.supports: Reading and acting on device notifications is listed as Android only.

sources.title: Node troubleshooting
sources.supports: The permissions matrix marks computer.act as not applicable on iOS and Android.

sources.title: AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.supports: iOS does not let an app use the camera while it is in the background.

sources.title: Handling location updates in the background (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.supports: iOS suspends most apps shortly after they leave the foreground and may terminate them at any time.

sources.title: Pushing background updates to your App (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.supports: Apple treats background pushes as low priority, does not guarantee delivery, may throttle them, and gives the app 30 seconds per wake.

removed.name: Look, don't touch: read a Mac's screen with input withheld

sources.supports: A hook can block a tool call outright based on its parameters.

sources.supports: Screen recording is its own per-app switch in Privacy & Security.

sources.supports: A paired node enters the computer tool's pool only if it advertises both the input command and the screen snapshot command.

removed.name: Show it on the Mac: a family board in the app's widget panel
removed.reason: A schedule card in the Mac app's floating panel cannot be triggered from iMessage or from a scheduled job, and no Mac in the house is a screen the family looks at.

sources.title: Widget panel
sources.supports: The recommended agent path is show_widget targeting the node panel, which opens the app's native panel on a connected Mac.

sources.title: Node command policy: plugin defaults

sources.title: show_widget: Show on a device
sources.supports: If no eligible Mac is connected the widget still appears inline in chat.

sources.title: macOS app: What the app owns
sources.supports: The app's single Mac node combines computer control, capture and the widget panel with the CLI node host's system, browser, plugin, skill and MCP commands.

sources.title: show_widget tool definition
sources.supports: Without a current-channel presenter or the pinned-only surface, the tool carries a required client capability.

removed.name: File chores by an allowlisted script on a Mac node (tidy Downloads)
removed.reason: Tidying a Downloads folder is better done by a weekly scheduled script with no agent at all; the agent route needs shell access on a parent's laptop.

sources.title: Run commands on a node

sources.title: Exec approvals: argPattern

sources.title: Run a node host: System commands
sources.supports: The macOS node exposes shell execution commands and commands that read and set its exec approvals, alongside notifications.

sources.title: Paired node desktops
sources.supports: CLI nodes share their desktop by default unless the setting is explicitly false.

removed.name: HappyDrop: one shared folder on a parent's Mac, file transfer only
removed.reason: A shared folder on a parent's Mac adds a new trust surface for something an iMessage attachment already does, and files are capped at 16 MiB.

sources.title: Node file transfers: Agent file transfers
sources.supports: Listing, fetching and writing are separate tools and allowing one does not expose the others.

sources.title: Run a node host: Restrict the node command surface
sources.supports: A node can be started so that it advertises only an explicit list of command ids.

sources.title: File Transfer plugin manifest
sources.supports: The plugin contributes four agent tools: file_fetch, dir_list, dir_fetch and file_write.

sources.supports: The file and directory node commands are registered as dangerous.

sources.title: Node command policy
sources.supports: Plugin node commands flagged dangerous stay blocked until listed in gateway.nodes.commands.allow.

removed.name: Full screen control of a parent's everyday MacBook
removed.reason: Full screen control of a parent's everyday laptop puts private data, an untrusted screen and every way out into one tool with no per-action confirmation.

sources.title: Computer use: Safety
sources.supports: Actions execute while the durable controls stay enabled, without confirmation for each one.

sources.title: Exec approvals: Trust model
sources.supports: A paired node carries gateway-operator trust onto that machine.

sources.title: Remote control
sources.supports: The macOS app can connect to a gateway on another host over the tailnet.

sources.title: Computer use tool: security considerations (Anthropic)
sources.supports: The vendor advises against giving the model access to sensitive data such as logins and asks for human confirmation of consequential actions.

sources.title: RedTeamCUA
sources.supports: Computer-use agents in a realistic test bed followed injected instructions in a substantial share of cases.

sources.title: Run a node host: System commands
sources.supports: The macOS node exposes shell execution commands and commands that read and set its exec approvals, alongside notifications.

removed.name: Fetch a document from a site that needs a parent's sign-in
removed.reason: Fetching documents from a signed-in portal would give a shared agent an account, and every expired session means signing in again by hand at the Mac, which is slower than downloading the file on a phone.

sources.title: Computer use: browser family
sources.supports: The CUA provider adds browser actions including navigation, typing, file inputs and downloads.

sources.title: Browser login
sources.supports: Manual sign-in is recommended because automated logins can trigger bot defences and lock accounts.

sources.title: Computer use guide (OpenAI)
sources.supports: The vendor recommends limiting computer use to an allowlist of sites and warns that it can affect real accounts.

sources.title: computer tool schema
sources.supports: The tool accepts a profile choice of a new or a named isolated profile, plus a url parameter a hook can inspect.

removed.name: What is that Mac doing? Presence at most, no screenshot journals
removed.reason: Knowing which Mac was used last answers no real family question, and the Logbook plugin behind the fuller version is continuous screen capture sent to a cloud model.

sources.title: Active computer presence
sources.supports: Presence indicates the most recently used Mac and is explicitly not proof of who sent a message.

sources.title: Logbook plugin
sources.supports: Logbook is bundled but off, and enabling it turns screen capture on.

sources.title: Family Sharing and parental controls overview for kids and teens (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Apple's built-in parental controls report a child's app and website activity and set schedules and limits.

sources.title: Presence
sources.supports: Agents read people and device presence through a core tool.

removed.name: Kitchen wall board in the style of Skylight or Hearth
removed.reason: A Skylight-style kitchen board would mean pairing a shared-room tablet as a gateway console that can open both parents' private conversations; a shared calendar on an old iPad or the printed sheet does the job.

sources.title: Skylight Calendar | The Digital Calendar for Busy Families
sources.supports: Skylight sells a wall calendar with tasks, reward stars, meal planning and import of events from forwarded emails and photos, with paid Plus features at 79 dollars a year.

sources.title: Hearth Display: Kids grow fast. Hearth grows with them.
sources.supports: Hearth sells a wall display with a family dashboard, visual kid routines with built-in rewards, meal planning and an AI helper.

sources.title: Meet Our Family Membership
sources.supports: Hearth's routines, to-dos, meal planning and AI helper sit behind a monthly membership.

sources.title: Show widget: scheduled surface
sources.supports: A scheduled automation bound to a persistent session may update pinned dashboard widgets without a connected client.

sources.title: Session dashboards
sources.supports: Each thread in the web UI can own a dashboard of widgets the agent builds.

sources.title: Operator scopes
sources.supports: A read-only operator scope exists for clients that should not send messages or invoke tools.

removed.name: Location and arrival alerts: use Find My, not Happy

sources.title: Locate people in Find My on Apple Watch - Apple Support
sources.supports: Find My can notify you when a person leaves their location or arrives at yours.

sources.title: Location command
sources.supports: Location is a node command invoked through the gateway, available only from a paired node.

sources.title: Channel location parsing
sources.supports: Shared-location parsing is listed for LINE, Matrix, Telegram and WhatsApp, not iMessage.

sources.title: Get notified when someone's location changes in Find My on Mac - Apple Support
sources.supports: Find My can alert you when a person arrives at, leaves or is not at a place, and the other person is told or must approve.

sources.title: iOS app: background alive beacons
sources.supports: When iOS wakes the app in the background it makes a brief reconnect and records a presence beacon.

sources.title: AI-powered tutor Khanmigo by Khan Academy (parents page)
sources.supports: The parent plan costs four dollars a month, covers up to ten children, guides rather than answers, and shows parents the chat history with flags.

sources.title: Guide your child's Gemini Apps experience - Gemini Apps Help
sources.supports: Google allows parents to enable Gemini for children under 13 through supervised accounts and lists its own cautions.

removed.name: Phone calls: call Happy, wake-up calls, calls to businesses
removed.reason: Calling Happy, wake-up calls and calls to businesses need either a public web address or weakened Mac security, so calls stay off.

sources.supports: A commercial assistant offers phoning the assistant and spoken wake-up calls.

sources.title: Voice call plugin: setup warning

sources.supports: The FaceTime integration uses private Apple APIs and needs weakened SIP protections.

sources.supports: A per-contact setting lets that contact's message sounds come through when other notifications are silenced.

removed.name: Agentic errands: reservations, orders, repair bookings

sources.supports: Alexa+ makes reservations and appointments, orders groceries and food, and can navigate a site to arrange a repair.

sources.title: Browser login
sources.supports: Automated logins often trigger bot defences and can lock an account, so manual sign-in is advised.

removed.name: Personal Gmail summaries and reply drafts: leave them to Gmail

sources.title: Gmail is entering the Gemini era
sources.supports: Thread summaries, Help Me Write and Suggested Replies are free for all Gmail users, while inbox-wide questions and Proofread need a paid Google AI plan.

sources.title: FaceTime plugin

sources.supports: Funnel routes traffic from the public internet to a local service, whereas Serve shares only inside the tailnet.

sources.title: Plugin inventory: sms

sources.title: Video generation

sources.supports: A bundled skill edits a chosen PDF page from a natural-language instruction.

sources.supports: nano-pdf edits PDF slides by sending page images and prompts to Google's Gemini image model and needs a paid Gemini API key.

removed.name: A parent's iPhone location and daily Health summary on request

sources.supports: The IMAP path hands the reader an email body capped at a byte limit with a truncation marker; nothing is said about images.

sources.title: Automation payloads: command output
