sources.title: Google Chrome Help: Fill out forms automatically in Chrome
sources.supports: The browser already stores and fills contact details, addresses and similar form data for the person using it.

sources.title: OpenAI API docs: Computer use
sources.supports: OpenAI's developer guidance: run the agent in an isolated browser with a list of permitted sites and actions, treat on-screen text as untrusted, keep the user in control of purchases and other hard-to-reverse steps, and treat typing sensitive data into a form as sending it.

sources.title: arXiv 2504.01382: An Illusion of Progress? Assessing the Current State of Web Agents
sources.supports: An independent evaluation on 300 live-website tasks found web agents much less competent than earlier benchmark results suggested.

sources.title: Browser control API: CLI quick reference
sources.supports: The browser tool can type into a field and submit in one step, which is why submit has to be blocked in code rather than by instruction.

sources.title: Tool call policy hooks
sources.supports: An approval requirement halts the run until a person decides.

removed.name: Utility bills and usage, read-only: bill emails plus a Green Button file
removed.reason: The bill-due line already exists in F060 and autopay covers most of it, and a usage analysis would need a parent to download a data file from the very portal that already shows the numbers.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Energy: Green Button
sources.supports: Green Button lets utility customers download their own usage data in a standard format after logging in to the utility portal; the automated variant transfers data only to third parties the customer authorises.

sources.title: Code execution
sources.supports: The code_execution tool is remote Python at a third-party provider, not local analysis.

sources.title: Media understanding: File-attachment extraction
sources.supports: In sandboxed sessions only PDF and plain-text attachments are promised to reach the model as text; other formats get an 'unsupported' marker, which is the risk for an XML usage export.

sources.title: IMAP email trigger: Sender authentication
sources.supports: Bill emails forwarded into the watched mailbox are accepted only if they pass the watcher's aligned DMARC check.

removed.name: Save a public page as a PDF (and why receipts are a mail job)
removed.reason: Saving a web page as a PDF takes two taps on a phone, printing included; the agent version needs new plumbing between the web-reading agent and the printer.

sources.title: Browser (OpenClaw-managed): What you get
sources.supports: The managed browser can produce PDFs of pages.

sources.title: Existing-session feature limitations
sources.supports: PDF export and downloads need a Playwright-backed managed profile.

sources.title: Browser control risks
sources.supports: Files that come out of the browser are untrusted input.

sources.title: PDF tool: Supported PDF references
sources.anchor: rejected when the tool runs sandboxed
sources.supports: The PDF analysis tool will not fetch remote links from a sandboxed session.

sources.title: Bundled skill: nano-pdf
sources.supports: nano-pdf is a PDF editing CLI, not a page-saving tool.

sources.title: Apple Support: Use AirPrint to print from your iPhone or iPad
sources.supports: An iPhone prints from an app's Share menu to an AirPrint printer on the same Wi-Fi network.

removed.name: Store stock check
removed.reason: A store stock check usually ends in 'could not verify' because retailer sites block automation, and the retailer's own app is faster and more accurate.

sources.title: Best Buy API documentation
sources.supports: One large retailer publishes an official keyed API that returns near-real-time store availability for a product by postal code.

sources.title: Cloudflare docs: Bot detection engines
sources.supports: A major bot-management vendor documents a detection engine aimed specifically at headless browsers.

sources.title: Web fetch: Limits and safety
sources.supports: The docs describe web_fetch as best effort, with some sites needing the browser.

sources.title: Bundled skill: ordercli
sources.supports: The bundled order-status skill supports a single food-delivery service.

removed.name: Bot-wall workarounds: stealth proxies, hosted browsers, CAPTCHA solving
removed.reason: Stealth proxies, hosted browsers and CAPTCHA solving stay off; Happy reports the block instead of working round it.

sources.title: Firecrawl
sources.supports: The Firecrawl integration is a hosted extraction service positioned for pages that block plain fetches.

sources.title: Remote and hosted browsers: Browserbase
sources.supports: A documented hosted-browser option advertises CAPTCHA solving, stealth and residential proxies.

sources.title: Browser login: Manual login
sources.supports: Automated logins are documented as likely to trigger bot defenses and lock accounts.

sources.title: Bundled skill: browser-automation
sources.supports: The bundled skill instructs the agent to stop and tell the user when a page needs a login, captcha or 2FA.

sources.title: Claude Help Center: Use Claude in Chrome safely
sources.supports: Anthropic lists getting past captchas among the things its own browser agent is not allowed to do.

sources.title: ACTIVE Network: Terms of Use
sources.supports: A large camp and activity registration platform prohibits automated access tools and treats automated processing of registrations beyond stated limits as a violation.

removed.name: Inbound iMessage attachments (photos, PDFs, voice memos)
removed.reason: Switching attachment intake on is one config line whose only job is to let Happy read what parents send, so it is the first step of photo and PDF reading (F002) and not a feature of its own. F003, CRT-15, MKT-02, SRC-14, MAC-07 and VOX-05 list F001 as a dependency and should point at F002.

sources.title: iMessage media and attachments
sources.supports: One channel switch forwards photos, voice memos and other attachments to the agent; it is the same switch photo and PDF reading needs before anything else.

removed.name: Spoken replies (TTS) and voice round trip
removed.reason: Spoken replies with the built-in say voice are the no-install first step of the job VOX-04 describes, and VOX-04 already lists say as one of its engines, so the two are one item. VOX-04 and VOX-01 list F004 as a dependency; VOX-01 should point at VOX-04.

sources.title: Text-to-speech configuration
sources.supports: The macOS say voice is one Local CLI preset of the same text-to-speech block that VOX-04's local neural voice configures.

sources.title: Use CarPlay with your iPhone - Apple Support
sources.supports: Siri already reads incoming messages aloud in the car, so the car case in this entry needs no audio file from Happy.

removed.name: Video clips sent to Happy
removed.reason: This entry records why Happy cannot watch videos with its current provider and lists options it does not itself recommend; its own review note says the honest deliverable is one line asking the sender for a photo. That line belongs in F002. Nothing depends on this entry.

sources.title: Media understanding
sources.supports: OpenClaw's bundled video-understanding providers are Google, Qwen and Moonshot, none of which this family uses, so there is no supported way to watch a clip on this setup.

removed.name: iMessage tapbacks, typing bubble, polls and tap-to-approve (Private API mode)
removed.reason: Tapbacks, typing bubbles, polls and tap-to-approve need System Integrity Protection switched off on the Mac that holds every family secret. OpenClaw's page recommends this mode in general but warns that turning SIP off is a real security tradeoff and says an install that cannot accept it is limited to basic text and media; the roadmap chose Basic mode with SIP on, and the entry itself says the gain is not worth it. Nothing depends on this entry.

sources.title: Enabling the imsg private API
sources.supports: OpenClaw warns that turning SIP off is a system-wide security tradeoff and says an install that cannot accept it is limited to basic text and media.

sources.title: About System Integrity Protection on your Mac (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Apple describes SIP as the protection that keeps malicious software, even with root access, from modifying protected files and folders.

removed.name: External calendar feeds (.ics): district calendar, team schedules, library and rec events
removed.reason: After the earlier reviews this entry is a setup step, not a feature: someone subscribes the family Google Calendar to public feed links by hand and Happy reads them through F009, while the fallback poller it mentions is SRC-09. CRT-11 lists G012 as a source for the district calendar and should point at F009.

sources.title: Subscribe to someone else's calendar (Google Calendar Help)
sources.supports: Adding a public calendar link is a manual Google Calendar step done in a computer browser; nothing in Happy has to be built for it.

sources.title: Subscribe to a Team Schedule - TeamSnap Playbook
sources.supports: Team schedules arrive as the same kind of calendar link and can lag by a day, which is the gap the SRC-09 change-alert job already covers.

removed.name: Notes and task apps as a filing target (Apple Notes, Obsidian, Things, Bear, Notion, Trello)
removed.reason: This is a survey of six bundled note and task skills that ends in a decision, not a feature: four apps are skipped, the Obsidian part is a person opening the shared folder with no agent involved, and the one buildable idea (adding to a shared Apple Note) has no tested method.

sources.title: apple-notes skill: limitations
sources.supports: The bundled Apple Notes skill warns that its command-line tool may need a terminal for interactive prompts, so it cannot be relied on for an unattended append.

sources.title: Skills: plugins and skills
sources.supports: A bundled skill is instructions only and gives an agent no tool, so listing six skills adds no capability by itself.

removed.name: Grocery list to an Instacart link, parent checks out
removed.reason: Instacart's developer programme is built for partner apps and websites, its own page says it is not taking new applications, and a key only works after a review it puts at about 30 to 40 days. The item's own notes also say a shared Reminders grocery list plus the store's own app already does this with nothing to build.

sources.title: Instacart Company | Instacart Developer Platform
sources.supports: Instacart describes the programme as mainly for partner apps and websites that serve consumers, and says it is not accepting new applications at present.

sources.title: Approval process | Instacart Docs
sources.supports: Asking for a production key starts a review of the integrator's app or website, and the key stays pending and does not work until that review is passed.

sources.title: Get started | Instacart Docs
sources.supports: Instacart puts the average time from access request to demo approval and a production key at roughly 30 to 40 days.

removed.name: Deep recall of earlier conversations (Active Memory)
removed.reason: It serves the same purpose as F041: answering 'what did we decide last week?'. F041 already saves each day's conversation into searchable notes, this item's own notes say to try that first, and with one conversation per parent this route may recall nothing at all.

sources.title: Bundled hooks: session-memory
sources.supports: The session-memory hook that F041 turns on already writes the ended day's conversation into the agent's memory notes at each reset, where memory search finds it.

sources.title: Enabling active memory: remember across conversations
sources.supports: Cross-conversation recall leaves out the conversation being answered, and each parent has only one conversation with their agent.

removed.name: IMAP mailbox watch on a personal Gmail (allowlisted senders, per-message reader)
removed.reason: Watching a personal Gmail this way needs a Google app password, which Google itself says is not recommended and which opens the whole account; the read-only sign-in in F047 reaches the same mail with a narrower grant. Other items lean on this one: F060 and F061 name this watch as their intake and F051 points to its delivery note, so those are repointed in the fold note.

sources.title: Sign in with app passwords - Google Account Help
sources.supports: Google says app passwords are not recommended, describes them as giving a less secure app access to the Google Account, and tells users to connect apps with Sign in with Google instead.

sources.title: IMAP email trigger
sources.anchor: Fastmail, iCloud, or another IMAP mailbox
sources.supports: OpenClaw's own guide presents this plugin for Fastmail, iCloud and similar mailboxes and takes only a mailbox password, with no Google sign-in option.

removed.name: Lost or stolen phone: lock one person out
removed.reason: Locking one person out is a second phrase on the same stop plugin as the kill switch (G005): same hooks, same wave, and this item already lists G005 as what it extends. One combined item covers both; nothing is lost.

sources.title: Plugin hooks: message hooks
sources.supports: Both the stop phrase and the lock-out phrase are claimed by the same plugin hook before the model sees the message, so they are one piece of code.

sources.title: Operator incident response: contain
sources.supports: OpenClaw's incident guide treats stopping the gateway and freezing who may message it as one containment step list.

removed.name: Guest tier: a grandparent or sitter can text Happy and gets a fridge-level card only
removed.reason: A sitter or visiting grandparent would be a lower-trust user on the parents' gateway: OpenClaw's security guidance says mixed-trust use belongs on a separate gateway, and on iMessage everyone admitted to chat is also on the list that may answer approval prompts. The record itself says most sitters will just text the parents, and a sitter is outside the 'messages go only to the family' rule; the sitter sheet (F036), translated when needed (G011) and forwarded by a parent, gives the same card. No other item depends on this one.

sources.title: Gateway security: one trust boundary per gateway
sources.supports: OpenClaw's guidance for people of different trust levels is to split them onto a separate gateway and credentials, not to share one.

sources.title: iMessage rich messages: approvals
sources.supports: On iMessage the admission list is also the approver list, so a guest who is let in to chat is also authorised to answer approval prompts.

removed.name: Standing orders: a written charter per recurring job
removed.reason: The charter for each job is rendered by the same generator, from the same family.json5 entries, as the jobs registry (G003), which this item names as its dependency. It is one piece of wave-A work, so it becomes part of G003. No item outside this group depends on it.

sources.title: Standing orders: how they work
sources.supports: OpenClaw describes the written program and the scheduled automation that fires it as one arrangement, which is what the registry generates.

removed.name: Unattended-job guardrails (failure alerts, auto-disable, missed runs)
removed.reason: By its own description this is the set of scheduler settings the jobs registry (G003) should be built on: a time limit and tool cap on every job the registry emits, plus three gateway switches. It is the same piece of wave-A work, so it becomes part of G003. AUT-01 and AUT-03 refer to it for the 'triggers off before any agent gets the automations tool' rule, which moves with it.

sources.title: openclaw automations: timeouts
sources.supports: The per-job time limit is a flag on the same add and edit command the registry generator emits, so the guardrail is part of generating the job.

sources.title: Automation delivery: failure notifications
sources.supports: Failure alerts are a built-in scheduler policy that only needs routing to the operator, a config line set once alongside the registry.

removed.name: Per-person and per-agent spend caps with a daily cost line
removed.reason: The caps and the alert already exist: every OpenAI project has a hard monthly limit and a Grafana rule alerts Tony when an agent passes its daily budget (happy-config baseline/caps-m1.md, confirmed 9 Oct). What is left is a rule, 'every new agent or key gets its own cap and budget line before it goes live', which is a line on the operator's checklist (OCL-13), not a feature. VOX-02 lists this item as a dependency and OCL-06, OCL-13 and CRT-04 mention it; they should point at that checklist line.

sources.title: OpenAI API guide: Spend limits
sources.supports: The hard stop is a setting on each OpenAI project, made once in the provider's dashboard; there is nothing for Happy to build.

sources.title: Prometheus metrics
sources.supports: The per-agent cost counter that the existing daily-budget alert reads is exported by the Gateway already.

removed.name: Nightly backups and a quarterly restore drill
removed.reason: Already running since M0: a verified archive of Happy's state every night at 03:15, 14 days kept, on the encrypted disk and in the encrypted Time Machine backup, and one restore drill passed. What is left is the roadmap's standing rule to repeat the drill each quarter and to add new stores to the backup set, which are lines on the operator's checklist (OCL-13), not a feature. CRT-05 lists 'G007 backups' as a dependency, which is already met; OCL-10 and OCL-13 only mention it.

sources.title: Backup CLI
sources.supports: The archive-and-verify step is one built-in command, which the existing nightly script already runs; nothing further has to be built.

sources.title: Apple Support: Back up your Mac with Time Machine
sources.supports: The encrypted off-disk copy is a macOS feature that is already switched on for this Mac.

removed.name: Apple Foundation Models as the free on-device utility model
removed.reason: Its own description says the family sees no difference: the Apple on-device model only writes session titles and progress notes on screens Happy does not use. The one use the catalog kept it for, a free local classifier behind the privacy gate, is not documented for it, and OCL-14 now covers local classification by a documented route. No other item depends on it.

sources.title: Agent model configuration
sources.supports: The utility model powers Control UI session titles, activity recaps and progress narration, none of which appear in an iMessage thread.

sources.title: Decision models: roles
sources.supports: Classification is the documented job of the decision-model role, which OCL-14 fills with a local provider.

removed.name: Weekday morning brief (07:00, no mail yet)
removed.reason: This is the same job as the evening brief on a different schedule: the same calendar and weather, the same tools, built in the same piece of work. It becomes the optional 07:00 schedule of the combined briefs entry (F014).

sources.title: Keep the Family Up to Date with Daily Agenda Emails | Cozi Family Organizer
sources.supports: Cozi sends family members a morning email of the day's calendar events and offers the weekly agenda as a second setting of the same feature, which is how the combined briefs entry now treats them.

sources.title: CLI reference: automations (cron)
sources.supports: Each brief is one scheduled agent job created from a cron line, so the morning, evening and Sunday briefs differ only in schedule and prompt.

removed.name: Sunday 18:00 week-ahead
removed.reason: This is the same job as the evening brief with a Sunday schedule and a seven-day window: the same calendar and weather, the same tools, built in the same piece of work. It becomes the Sunday 18:00 schedule of the combined briefs entry (F014).

sources.title: Wish You Had an Instant Way To Tell Everyone the Family’s Weekly Plan? (Cozi blog)
sources.supports: Cozi's weekly agenda email goes to chosen family members on Sundays with the week's events, a second schedule of the same agenda feature as its daily email.

sources.title: Automation schedules
sources.supports: A brief's schedule is one cron expression in a named time zone, so the Sunday week-ahead is the evening brief's job with a different line.

removed.name: Overnight interest brief on the research agent
removed.reason: The entry itself says to skip it if a parent uses Gemini or Google Alerts, and Gemini already does daily topic tracking for up to ten topics. The catalog had already dropped this kind of topic brief once, and its one example (a registration date opening) is the page watcher's job (F029).

sources.title: Schedule actions in Gemini Apps - Gemini Apps Help
sources.supports: Gemini already offers daily topic tracking and news digests as scheduled actions, up to ten at a time, with or without a paid Google AI plan.

removed.name: Family week board in the Control UI (pinned native report)
removed.reason: The board lives in OpenClaw's Control UI, which the vendor calls an admin surface, so in practice only Tony could open it, and it cannot be shown in iMessage. The entry itself says the phones' calendar widgets and the evening and Sunday briefs already cover it; four earlier board entries (AUT-10, HOM-10, MKT-09, MAC-08) were removed for the same reasons.

sources.title: Dashboard (Control UI) access and auth
sources.supports: The vendor describes the Control UI, where the board would live, as an admin surface for chat, config and approvals, not a page to hand to the rest of the family.

sources.title: Show widget: availability
sources.supports: Channel runs such as iMessage are not offered the widget tool, so the board can never be asked for or shown in the family's thread.

removed.name: Week sheet on paper as a no-model job
removed.reason: This is the Sunday fridge sheet that the printing entry (F080) already lists. The only thing it adds is a build detail: producing the sheet with a plain scheduled script and no model call.

sources.title: Automation payloads: command payloads
sources.supports: A scheduled command can run a script with no model call; that is the one thing this entry adds, and it is a build choice for the fridge sheet F080 already includes.

removed.name: Urgent school alert relay (snow day, delay, early dismissal, bus, safety)
removed.reason: The school's own alert system already sends closures and delays straight to both parents' phones and cannot be muted, so Happy's relay would arrive second, and a wrong 'routine' label could hide a closure. The one useful rule (do not hold an urgent school email until 16:00) moves into the school digest (F056); OCL-14 names this relay as a user of its classifier and SRC-08 calls it a backup, so both should point to F056.

sources.title: ParentSquare: Help Please! Frequently Asked Parent Questions
sources.supports: A widely used school messaging vendor says urgent alerts and attendance notices always come through whatever the parent's notification setting, and that only the school can stop them.

removed.name: School platform feed map: what each system really sends
removed.reason: This is a setup recipe and a record of what each school system sends, not something Happy does by itself: a parent sets each platform's notification options once and the result shows up only inside the school digest. It moves into that entry (F056) as its per-platform setup. No other entry depends on it; the line another review folds in here (IPH-15) travels with it.

sources.title: PowerSchool SIS student and parent help: Email Notifications
sources.supports: What this entry describes is a parent filling in the platform's own notification settings once, including an extra recipient address, which is a setup step for the school mailbox and its digest.

sources.title: ParentSquare: Help Please! Frequently Asked Parent Questions
sources.supports: ParentSquare's evening Digest is a setting the parent chooses per school, again a one-time configuration and not an agent feature.

removed.name: Google Classroom guardian summaries in the school digest
removed.reason: A Classroom guardian summary is one more email arriving in the school mailbox, and its whole result is one line inside the school digest, the same way the lunch-balance and library notices were handled earlier. It becomes a sender in F056 instead of a separate entry; it also only applies if the school uses Google Classroom, which nobody has checked.

sources.title: Get Classroom email summaries (for guardians) - Classroom Help
sources.supports: The guardian summary is an ordinary email that can go to any address, so in the school mailbox it is one more school message for the existing digest to read.

removed.name: School lunch menu answers (no documented feed)
removed.reason: There is no documented menu feed to watch, and the menu vendor's own site and app already show the current menu, while a once-a-month import would sometimes be wrong and Happy must never be the allergy authority. If a parent does send the monthly menu, that is ordinary snap-to-action (F011) and needs no entry of its own; the lunch-balance line already lives in the school digest (F056).

sources.title: Nutrislice: K-12 school foodservice solutions
sources.supports: The menu vendor already puts each school's menu online and on phones for parents, and its product page mentions no feed, API or calendar subscription a home agent could read.

sources.title: Web fetch
sources.supports: Happy's page reader does not run JavaScript, so a script-rendered menu page would return no menu to it.

removed.name: Practice drills: spelling lists, math facts, reading buddy and bedtime story
removed.reason: The parent-run drills are the same thing as the practice quiz in MKT-02 with a typed list in place of a photo, and the entry itself says a parent can already run them from their own chat. The version the kids would use themselves cannot exist before the kids agent (F072), and 'reading buddy' and 'bedtime story' were named but never described.

sources.title: Introducing Alexa+, the next generation of Alexa
sources.supports: The products that ship this treat it as one function, a quiz made from whatever material the user supplies, so a typed spelling list and a photographed study guide are the same feature.

sources.title: Session management
sources.supports: The running score is just conversation state that lasts until the daily reset, so the drills need nothing built beyond the quiz prompt.

removed.name: Kid-safe weekly card baked into the kids agent
removed.reason: The printed Sunday fridge sheet already shows the kids the week's schedule and chore turns, the paediatricians' advice is a chart posted where the child sees it, and the product that sells this to families is a wall display, not a chat for children. A chat version would also put the family's weekly schedule into the kids agent, which the roadmap describes as holding nothing to steal, and it needs a calendar reader and a notes store that do not exist. Nothing depends on it (OCL-03 and HOM-14 only list it as an overlap).

sources.title: Age-Appropriate Chores for Children - HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics)
sources.supports: The paediatricians' guidance is a chore list posted in the child's room or on the refrigerator, which the printed week sheet provides without a chat agent.

sources.title: Skylight Calendar | Smart Family Calendar
sources.supports: The product that sells this to families does it as a shared family display showing each person's events and chores, not as a chat agent for children.

removed.name: Kid check-in relay and kid-side chore done
removed.reason: A child who has an Apple account to text Happy can text a parent or the family chat directly, the iPhone's own Check In can tell a parent automatically when the child's phone has arrived, and Family Sharing shows the device in Find My. The record itself says no source shows kids would text the agent instead of a parent. Nothing else depends on it (CRT-03 only borrowed the hook shape).

sources.title: Use Check In for Messages on iPhone (Apple Support)
sources.supports: The iPhone's Messages app can tell a chosen person automatically that the phone has arrived, which is the 'I'm home' relay without an agent in the middle.

sources.title: Family Sharing - Apple
sources.supports: Family Sharing members can share their location and show their devices in Find My, so a parent can already see whether a child's device is at home.

sources.title: Create an Apple Account for your child
sources.supports: A parent creates the child's own Apple Account, the same step that would give the child a handle to text Happy in the first place.

removed.name: Birthday, anniversary and gift-date heads-up
removed.reason: The phones already do the core of this: birthdays saved in contacts appear in the calendar by themselves, and the iPhone calendar can alert up to a week ahead. What is left (anniversary and gift dates with last year's gift note) is a few more rows in the dated-reminders list (F063), not a separate daily job with its own hand-entered table. Nothing depends on it.

sources.title: Manage birthdays on your calendar (Google Calendar Help)
sources.supports: Birthdays saved in Google Contacts show up in the person's Google Calendar automatically, with nothing to enter twice.

sources.title: How to Change the Default Reminder Time in Calendar (iPhone Life)
sources.supports: The iPhone Calendar has a default alert for birthdays that can be set to the day itself, one or two days before, or one week before.

removed.name: Pending items view: approvals waiting, drafts unsent, watchers, reminders, open requests
removed.reason: Once the parts that cannot work are taken out (gateway approvals lapse within ten minutes, and unsent drafts belong to the later mail work), what is left today is the list of scheduled reminders, which the reminders entry (F007) already promises; page watchers would show up in that same list. Open requests and proposals awaiting a yes would need tables that do not exist. Nothing depends on it (OCL-06 and CRT-01 only mention it as an overlap).

sources.title: Manage automations
sources.supports: The same automations list that F007 uses to list reminders returns every scheduled job with its name and next run time, which is the working core of a what-is-pending answer.

sources.title: Plugin permission requests
sources.supports: Approval requests expire after ten minutes at most, so there is no day-long queue of waiting approvals to show.

removed.name: Fact check and official-source answers
removed.reason: A fact check is the research helper answering under the citation and freshness rules (F022); the record's own build note says its rubric is folded into the F022 section, so there is nothing separate to build. Nothing depends on it.

sources.title: Web fetch: limits and safety
sources.supports: Config offers only a hostname denylist, so 'official sites only' is not a setting; the fact check adds no mechanism beyond the search, fetch and citation rules the research entries already hold.

removed.name: Find a place and route errands: open-now dinner, urgent care, pharmacy, Saturday loop
removed.reason: This is the Places lookup (F021) with an answer format: the same Google Places search, the same open-now and rating filters, the same Maps link. The record also concedes that phone maps apps already answer these questions with live traffic, so it does not earn a separate entry; nothing depends on it.

sources.title: Bundled goplaces skill
sources.supports: The open-now and minimum-rating search this entry describes is the same bundled Places command that F021 wraps.

removed.name: Feed watch for school, PTA, town and library sites (RSS/Atom)
removed.reason: This is the same job as the page watcher (F029): tell the parents when a public school, town or library site posts something new. F029 already says to use a site's own feed first, so the two are one piece of work in the same wave; no other item depends on this one.

sources.title: Bundled skill: blogwatcher
sources.supports: The feed tool this item is built on is the same one already cited on the page watcher, whose order of preference starts with a site's own feed.

sources.title: Automation payloads
sources.supports: Both watchers come down to one scheduled host command with no model in it, so they are one script and one job pattern.

removed.name: Grocery and errand capture by text or voice, plus Saturday shop list
removed.reason: Texting 'add oat milk' is exactly what the shared Reminders bridge (F030) does, and the item's own Apple source says the iPhone already sorts a grocery list by itself. Only the Saturday list text is new, and it fits as one optional job under F030; WEB-11, MKT-05 and SRC-04 use the grocery list and should point to F030.

sources.title: Create grocery lists in Reminders on your iPhone - Apple Support
sources.supports: The iPhone's Reminders app already keeps a grocery list and sorts it into store sections, so capture and sorting need nothing beyond the list bridge.

removed.name: Draft-only outreach texts (vendors, coaches, carpool parents)
removed.reason: Asking Happy to word a text to the plumber or the coach is ordinary chat that works today with nothing to build; what the item really records is the rule that Happy never sends to anyone outside the family, which the family delivery item (G009) already states. CRT-10 mentions it for a draft absence note, which still works without this item.

sources.title: Tool policy (OpenClaw docs)
sources.supports: The only mechanism on the item is that the parent's agent is not granted the send tool, which is the family-only rule and not a feature of its own.

removed.name: Kids' chore rota and after-school routine board (parent-run)
removed.reason: The kids are not users, so this board would only text the parents, and the item itself says a paper chart on the fridge may be less effort. The paediatricians' advice it cites is exactly that, a chore list posted in the child's room or on the refrigerator, which the Sunday fridge sheet (F080) can print; only OCL-03 mentions this entry, as an overlap.

sources.title: Age-Appropriate Chores for Children - HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics)
sources.supports: The paediatricians' advice is a star chart or chore list posted where the child sees it, in their room or on the refrigerator; that is a sheet of paper, not texts to a parent.

removed.name: Document vault: 'file this' (insurance, warranties, manuals)
removed.reason: The parts a parent would notice are already elsewhere: the reminder before a policy or warranty expires is the renewals program (F063), the short summary is a page in the family vault (F043), and appliance manuals belong to the home registry (F034). What is left is a new tool to copy the PDF onto the Mac, while the paperwork kit (CRT-12) already keeps scans in the phone's Files; OCL-08 and CRT-12 mention this entry only as an overlap.

sources.title: openclaw wiki CLI reference (OpenClaw docs)
sources.supports: The vault cannot hold the PDF itself, only a text summary, so everything except a new file-copy tool is already covered by the vault and the renewals list.

removed.name: 'Did I get an email about X?' lookup and thread summary
removed.reason: This is what the read-only Gmail connection (F047) is for: a parent asks 'did the dentist confirm?' and their mail agent searches their own inbox, in the same wave and the same piece of work. It becomes F047's example instead of a second item; the thread-summary half is free inside Gmail now, and no other item depends on this one.

sources.title: Bundled gog skill
sources.supports: The lookup uses only the Gmail search and read commands that the read-only connection already gives the owner's mail agent.

sources.title: Gmail is entering the Gemini era (Google, January 2026)
sources.supports: Google says conversation summaries of long email threads are free for every Gmail user, while asking the whole inbox a question needs a paid plan; so the lookup is the part worth keeping, and it is F047.

removed.name: Draft a reply or note (lands in Gmail Drafts)
removed.reason: Gmail now writes reply drafts by itself at no cost, inside the thread the owner must open anyway to press send, and Happy's version would need a Google token that is able to send; the catalog's earlier round already said to leave personal reply drafts to Gmail. It is the Gmail drafts connection (F048) described a second time, so it goes the same way, and the morning digest (F016) should not point here for drafts.

sources.title: Gmail is entering the Gemini era (Google, January 2026)
sources.supports: Google says Help Me Write and Suggested Replies, which draft a reply inside the thread, are rolling out free to every Gmail user: the job this item would do.

sources.title: Gmail API: Choose scopes
sources.supports: The permission that lets an agent write a draft is the same one that lets it send, so Happy's version needs a token that could always send mail.

sources.title: gogcli command reference: gog gmail drafts reply
sources.anchor: Save a reply as a draft
sources.supports: The reply draft would be made by the same gog drafts commands that F048 wraps, so there is no separate mechanism here.

removed.name: Appointment, refill, results and travel-change emails to .ics, reminders and alerts
removed.reason: Each part repeats something the parent's phone already does: Google Calendar adds flights, reservations and ticketed or medical events from Gmail by itself, Apple Calendar suggests events it finds in Mail, and the pharmacy, clinic and airline emails are themselves the alerts. Happy's version would put a watcher on a private inbox, health mail included, to send them a second time; its absorbed bill-due line stays with the morning mail digest (F016), and CRT-10 and CRT-14 mention this entry only as an overlap.

sources.title: Manage your events from Gmail - Google Calendar Help
sources.supports: Google Calendar already adds events from Gmail automatically: flights and other travel, hotel and restaurant reservations, and ticketed or registered events including medical ones.

sources.title: Apple Support: Use Siri Suggestions in Calendar on Mac
sources.supports: Apple's Calendar already picks up events it recognises in Mail and offers them as suggestions.

removed.name: Vehicle recall check by make, model and year (NHTSA)
removed.reason: NHTSA's own free SaferCar app already sends recall alerts for the exact car by its VIN, and for car seats and tires, while Happy's version can only match make, model and year and still has to send the parent off to a VIN check. Nothing else in the catalog depends on this entry.

sources.title: SaferCar on the App Store (developer: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration)
sources.supports: NHTSA's own app takes each vehicle's VIN, plus equipment such as tires and car seats, and notifies the owner of safety recalls on exactly those items.

sources.title: NHTSA's New SaferCar App Aims to Stop Deadly Recall Notification Delays (Consumer Reports)
sources.supports: A recall often covers only some trims or build periods, so an alert tied to the VIN is more accurate than one tied to make, model and year.

sources.title: NHTSA recalls API, live response
sources.supports: The public interface Happy would poll answers by make, model and model year only, so it lists every campaign for the model and cannot say whether this car is affected.

removed.name: Explain this EOB or medical bill
removed.reason: This is the general 'Explain this' feature (F023) pointed at one kind of document: the same photo or PDF in, the same five-line answer out, and nothing extra to build. The medical-bill wording moves into F023. Nothing else depends on this entry.

sources.title: Media understanding
sources.supports: A medical bill arrives through the same generic path as any other attached document, as extracted text wrapped for the reply model, with no bill-specific mechanism.

sources.title: How to read a health insurance explanation of benefits
sources.supports: The federal guide lists the fixed fields an Explanation of Benefits carries, which is all the line template carried into F023 needs.

removed.name: School, camp and sports health-form helper
removed.reason: The enrolment and camp paperwork kit (CRT-12) already promises the copy-paste answers for these forms and names this entry as the piece that supplies them, so the helper is folded into the kit instead of standing alone. Its four sources only show that attachments and prompts work, not a separate family need.

sources.title: Media understanding
sources.supports: A form photo or PDF reaches the model through the ordinary attachment path, so the helper is a prompt template over stored facts and not a separate capability.

removed.name: Pet care program
removed.reason: Nothing here is new work: a monthly dose reminder is an ordinary recurring reminder (F007), vaccine due dates are rows in the renewals look-ahead (F063), and the vet's number belongs in the provider registry (F034). The entry also admits no pet is mentioned in the household. Nothing else depends on it.

sources.title: Automation schedules
sources.supports: The monthly pet reminder is a plain recurring scheduled job, the same mechanism the timed-reminders feature already uses.

sources.title: Keep the Worms Out of Your Pet's Heart! The Facts about Heartworm Disease
sources.supports: Heartworm preventives are given monthly all year with a yearly test, which is one recurring reminder and one dated row, not a separate feature.

removed.name: Spend summary from statements (read-only, local model)
removed.reason: The entry itself questions whether dropping in monthly statements is worth it when bank and card apps already sort spending, and a card issuer's own assistant does send spending summaries and recurring-charge alerts straight from the live account. The wait for a local model is not the reason for removal. Nothing else depends on this entry.

sources.title: Eno, your Capital One assistant | Capital One
sources.supports: A card issuer's own assistant sends cardholders spending insights and summaries and flags items such as free trials and recurring charges, straight from the live account.

removed.name: Computer-control substrate: OpenClaw.app as the Mac node
removed.reason: Installing the OpenClaw Mac app gives the family nothing by itself; it is the first setup step of the screen-control pilot, so it is folded into that one entry (MAC-02). MAC-02, MAC-03, MAC-05 and MAC-07 list it as a dependency; MAC-03 should point to MAC-02 instead.

sources.title: Computer use: Requirements
sources.supports: A paired node that advertises the screenshot and input commands is listed as a requirement of the computer tool, which makes the app install a setup step of screen control and not a capability of its own.

removed.name: Watch Happy work: Screen Sharing and the Control UI Desktop panel
removed.reason: Watching the desk over Screen Sharing is a setup step of the screen-control pilot, and the entry itself says it has no value to the family on its own; it is folded into the pilot (MAC-02). Nothing else depends on it.

sources.title: Computer use
sources.anchor: not ordinary Gateway or paired-node desktops
sources.supports: The built-in pause when a person takes control exists only for cloud desktops, so on a paired Mac the watching view is an aid to a pilot run and not a control or feature of its own.

removed.name: Computer-use acceptance test: ten household tasks before any go-live
removed.reason: This is the pass-or-fail test for the screen-control pilot, not something the family uses, and it cannot run until the pilot's other pieces exist; it becomes the pilot's go-live gate inside MAC-02. MAC-07 lists it as a dependency and is removed in the same round.

sources.title: Computer use: Requirements
sources.supports: The computer tool needs a paired node, a vision model and a tool-policy grant before it runs at all, so a test of it can only be built as part of the same pilot work.

removed.name: Operate one Mac app that has no API (pilot: fill a flat PDF form)
removed.reason: The entry itself says Preview on a parent's Mac already fills and signs these forms with no agent and that a parent is usually faster by hand, while the screen-control route would send a child's health and insurance details to a cloud model as screenshots. The useful part, ready-to-paste answers for a form, is already F067.

sources.title: Fill out and sign PDF forms in Preview on Mac (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Apple's own Preview app fills PDF forms, offers a text box for forms that will not accept typing and adds a signature, so the same job is done on a parent's Mac with no agent.

sources.title: Computer use tool: Limitations (Anthropic)
sources.supports: A model vendor tells developers not to use computer use for tasks that need perfect precision or involve sensitive user information without human oversight; placing text on a scanned form of a child's health details is both.

sources.title: Computer use guide (OpenAI)
sources.supports: The family's model vendor treats typing sensitive information into a form as sending data out, an action a person is expected to confirm.

removed.name: Phone-node command ceiling: deny first, then pair
removed.reason: This is the 'deny first' step of pairing a phone, and the pairing entries already repeat nearly all of it (limited setup codes, Gateway-wide allow and deny lists, keeping agents away from the phone). It becomes step 1 of the single iPhone-app entry (OCL-01); nothing else depends on it, and with no phone paired today nothing is left unguarded in the meantime.

sources.title: Node command policy
sources.supports: One Gateway-wide deny list overrides every platform default and allow entry, so the phone ceiling is the same config list that MAC-04 and the pairing entry already edit.

sources.title: Node command policy
sources.supports: The setting that makes the Gateway ignore tools published by paired phones is the same one OCL-01 already tells the operator to set.

removed.name: Pair an iPhone as an OpenClaw node (official iOS app)
removed.reason: Pairing the iPhone app and using the iPhone app are one install and one setup code on the same phone, and OCL-01 already describes that pairing, so they are kept as one entry under OCL-01. IPH-02 and IPH-04 list this as a dependency and VOX-01 needs the same pairing; they should point to OCL-01, and IPH-02 keeps its own spare-phone notes if it survives.

sources.title: openclaw qr: Setup code contents
sources.supports: One setup code issues the phone's node token and its operator chat session together, so pairing the node and getting the chat app are a single step.

sources.title: iOS app: What it does
sources.supports: The same official app is described as both the device node and the chat surface, which is why the two entries describe one install.

removed.name: Read a parent's calendar, reminders, contacts and step count from their phone
removed.reason: The entry concedes that the phone's own Calendar and Reminders apps and Siri already answer these questions and that the Mac-side calendar (F009) is the dependable source: a parent texting from Messages has the OpenClaw app in the background, where iOS may suspend it, so the phone would often not answer. It would also need the Gateway app on each parent's personal phone, which OpenClaw says is not a boundary between people; calendar, reminders and contacts stay with F009, F030 and G013, and nothing depends on it.

sources.title: iOS app: pairing
sources.supports: The vendor says iOS may suspend the phone's node connection once the app goes to the background, which is where it sits while a parent is typing in Messages.

sources.title: iOS app: Computer Use relationship
sources.supports: Node commands sent to an iPhone are subject to iOS foreground and background limits, so on-demand reads from a pocketed phone are not dependable.

sources.title: Operator scopes
sources.supports: The vendor says operator scopes do not separate people on one Gateway, so pairing each parent's personal phone conflicts with keeping the two adults apart.

removed.name: Spare iPhone as a fixed camera
removed.reason: The entry itself says a cheap network camera or a doorbell's own app does this job better and the spare phone only wins on price; a free camera app for spare phones even adds motion alerts, which this route cannot. The phone would also have to sit in a window with the app held on screen around the clock while carrying a login that can read every conversation on the gateway, the same problem that removed the kitchen phone earlier.

sources.title: Camera capture: iOS foreground requirement
sources.supports: The iPhone node answers camera commands only while the app is in the foreground, so a camera phone must keep the app on screen at all times.

sources.title: AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground (Apple Developer Documentation, page data)
sources.supports: iOS does not let any app use the camera while it is in the background.

sources.title: What you get with a Nest Aware subscription (Google Nest Help)
sources.supports: A shipping doorbell product lists package detection as a built-in feature, which is the job this entry would give a spare phone.

sources.title: AlfredCamera | Simple Security at Your Fingertips
sources.supports: A shipping app already turns a spare phone into a security camera with motion detection and alerts, which a one-still-on-request route through Happy does not offer.

removed.name: iPhone Shortcuts automations as triggers for Happy
removed.reason: The entry concedes that Find My and Focus already cover arrive and leave alerts and that a plain schedule on the gateway already delivers its own example (pickup notes on weekday afternoons). What is left would switch on gateway web hooks with one shared secret stored on each parent's phone, the same design already turned down for HOM-06.

sources.title: Inbound webhooks
sources.anchor: Wake text is a system event
sources.supports: OpenClaw warns that hook wake text reaches the agent as a system event, not a safety-wrapped reader turn, and should carry only a short notification the operator controls.

sources.title: Hooks configuration reference
sources.supports: The gateway has one hook token shared by every caller, so both parents' phones would hold the same secret and the hook could not tell them apart.

sources.title: Get notified when someone's location changes in Find My on Mac (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Find My already notifies a person when a family member arrives at, leaves or is not at a place, including as a recurring notification, which covers the arrive and leave triggers.

removed.name: An idle Android phone that Happy can actually operate
removed.reason: The entry's own notes say the school and team apps already notify both parents' iPhones and that weekly use would not justify a second phone ecosystem in an all-Apple house. It needs an Android phone and a Google account the family does not own, kept signed in to those apps while a model taps through whatever other people post there, and OpenClaw documents the feature only as one line in a policy table.

sources.title: Node command policy
sources.supports: The only installed doc text on Android screen control is a note that the phone advertises it while Accessibility Control is on; there is no guide page describing it as a supported use.

sources.title: Claude API docs: Computer use tool
sources.supports: Model-vendor safety guidance says to avoid giving a screen-driving model access to account logins, which a phone kept signed in to the school and team apps would be.

removed.name: Relay notifications from chosen apps (Android only)
removed.reason: Both parents already get these notifications on their own iPhones, and the entry itself says the school mailbox route is simpler and needs no extra phone. On the gateway a forwarded notification arrives as trusted system text in a session the phone picks (a parent's private agent by default), which is the lane OpenClaw says to keep for text you control.

sources.title: Inbound webhooks
sources.anchor: Wake text is a system event
sources.supports: OpenClaw says system-event text is not a safety-wrapped reader turn and should carry only a short notification the operator controls; untrusted content belongs with a restricted reader.

sources.title: Gateway source: node events
sources.supports: A forwarded Android notification is queued as a system event on the session key the phone supplies, or on the system main session when none is set.

sources.title: Android app: Notification forwarding
sources.supports: Notification forwarding exists only in the Android app and is switched on at the phone, so it needs an Android device the family does not own.

removed.name: Accessibility routes: Switch Control and Voice Control
removed.reason: This is a record of a rejected idea, not a feature. Apple's Switch Control and Voice Control are built for a person, offer no interface a program can use, and a phone that obeys any voice in the room cannot be limited to the parents.

sources.title: Use Switch Control on your device to control another Apple device (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Switch Control lets a person with a switch operate another Apple device on the same network and account; the page describes no scripting or automation interface.

sources.title: Use Voice Control on your iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Voice Control is operated by a person speaking commands at the phone's microphone.

sources.title: Node troubleshooting
sources.supports: OpenClaw's permissions table marks screen control as not applicable on iOS.

removed.name: Screen Time and app requests by chat
removed.reason: The entry says this cannot and should not be done: Apple sends Screen Time and app requests to a parent's own Messages, only an adult set as parent or guardian can answer, and approving a child's downloads is a purchase action on the never list. Approving takes one tap on the parent's phone.

sources.title: Approve your child's purchases, downloads, and Screen Time requests (Apple Support)
sources.supports: Requests arrive in the approving adult's Messages with fixed approve choices, and only an adult set as parent or guardian can respond.

sources.title: iMessage channel: status
sources.supports: Anything beyond plain text and media on iMessage needs the private API mode, which this install does not run.

removed.name: A child's own device: school Chromebook, tablet, game console
removed.reason: This is an answer to a question, not a feature: a school Chromebook is managed by the school, and Family Link and Nintendo's controls live in the vendors' own parent apps, which already send reports to both parents. Any workaround would put a parent's vendor login, which can approve purchases, in an agent's hands.

sources.title: Learn on a school-managed Chromebook (Chromebook Help)
sources.supports: On a school Chromebook with a school account the school sets the limits and parents cannot add their own controls.

sources.title: Learn which devices can be supervised (Google For Families Help)
sources.supports: Family Link supervision is run from the parent's own app and covers Android and ChromeOS devices.

sources.title: Parental Controls App (Nintendo US)
sources.supports: Switch limits and reports are managed from Nintendo's phone app on the guardians' own devices.

removed.name: Browser action firewall hook (profile pin, site allowlist, approval before typing, no submit)
removed.reason: Folded, not dropped: the only browser left in the catalog is the research agent's (F020), built in the same wave, and this hook is what keeps that browser read-only, so the two are one piece of work. Its ask-before-typing branch belongs to the roadmap's M6 jobs agent (roadmap rule: site allowlist, approval before every form interaction, no submit), since the logged-in browser items it would have served here were already removed; no item depends on it, and the WEB-01 caveat that names it should point to F020.

sources.title: Tool call policy hooks
sources.supports: The mechanism is a before_tool_call hook that can block a call or pause it for approval, which F020 already names as its way to block typing and form filling in the research browser.

sources.title: Plugin hooks reference: timeouts and failures
sources.supports: A before_tool_call handler that throws or times out blocks the tool call, the fail-closed behaviour the merged F020 entry relies on.

removed.name: Voice guardrails pack (scoped devices, Talk owner, spoken confirmation)
removed.reason: Folded, not dropped: each limit in this pack already sits in the item it protects (the pairing profile in the iPhone app entry, the Talk owner in VOX-01, spoken confirmation in VOX-02, cloud speech off in VOX-04), and the room voice devices it was written for were removed earlier. VOX-01, VOX-02 and VOX-08 list it as a dependency and VOX-04 cites it, so its two remaining pieces move into VOX-01, the first voice surface, and those entries should point there.

sources.title: openclaw qr
sources.supports: The read-plus-talk pairing profile at the centre of this pack is meant for an embedded or room voice client, a device type the catalog no longer contains; the phone pairing entry already records the same profile choice.

sources.title: Operator scopes
sources.supports: OpenClaw says the read scope that every pairing profile carries is not a privacy boundary between people, so no setting in the pack separates the two adults.

sources.title: Talk mode
sources.supports: The Talk owner is a single gateway key that VOX-01 already has to set, so it belongs with Talk mode and not in a separate pack.

removed.name: Cooking companion by voice (hands-free kitchen session)
removed.reason: Cooking by voice is ordinary Talk mode (VOX-01) with a kitchen reply style, not a separate capability. The item's own notes say a Siri timer does the timing better and that a kitchen with children is the worst place for an open microphone feeding a cloud agent.

sources.title: Talk mode
sources.anchor: Native Talk is a continuous loop
sources.supports: Talk mode already is the listen, answer, speak loop the cooking session would run on; nothing new is switched on.

sources.title: Talk on macOS and the Gateway relay
sources.supports: The vendor advises headphones when a microphone stays open during playback, the opposite of a phone propped on a kitchen counter.

removed.name: Parent talks to Happy from the Apple Watch
removed.reason: Dictating an ordinary iMessage to Happy from the Watch already works with nothing to build, and the item itself names that as the path to use. The vendor's standalone Watch voice needs a gateway address reachable outside the tailnet, which the house rules forbid, and the companion app only rides on the operator's iPhone pairing.

sources.title: iOS app: standalone voice
sources.supports: The vendor says standalone Watch voice does not work away from the phone on a tailnet-only gateway, which is the only kind this house allows.

sources.title: Write messages on Apple Watch - Apple Support
sources.supports: Messages on the Watch already lets a parent dictate a text to Happy's contact, with no app, pairing or new credential.

removed.name: Bundled device skills: what each one controls and how it signs in
removed.reason: This is a decision record about nine bundled skills, not something a parent would use; its own description calls it that. The two skills worth keeping are already the Hue and Sonos items.

sources.title: openhue bundled skill
sources.supports: Hue pairing needs a physical press on the bridge, and the bridge must be on the local network.

sources.title: OpenHue CLI setup
sources.supports: The setup command discovers the bridge, waits for the button press and saves the bridge address and key in a YAML file under the user's home folder.

sources.title: Philips Hue developer: Get started
sources.supports: The Hue API is served locally by the bridge and issues an application key only after the link button is pressed, as proof of physical access.

sources.title: sonoscli bundled skill
sources.supports: On macOS the Gateway's parent process needs the Local Network privacy permission or Sonos discovery fails.

removed.name: LG TV: off at bedtime, notice on screen
removed.reason: Switching the TV off by text is already the named example of the allowlisted-Shortcut item (F078), and the TV's own Power Off Timer handles a fixed nightly cut-off. Only the on-screen notice is new, and it needs a Home Assistant server the house does not have.

sources.title: [LG TV Settings] How do I set a power on/off timer?
sources.supports: LG's own settings switch the TV off at a set time with a repeat option, so the scheduled cut-off needs no agent.

sources.title: Run shortcuts from the command line (Shortcuts User Guide for Mac)
sources.supports: The 'TV off' route is a named Shortcut run from the command line, which is exactly what F078 already provides.

removed.name: Is anyone home? (house-level presence)
removed.reason: The kids have no phones, so 'is anyone home?' only means 'is the other parent home?', which Find My already answers and can send alerts for. Happy's version needs a Home Assistant server plus a tracking app and VPN on both phones, and it reads 'nobody home' when the kids are in with a sitter. Nothing else in the catalog depends on it.

sources.title: Get notified when someone's location changes in Find My on Mac
sources.anchor: arrives at or leaves a location
sources.supports: Apple's Find My already tells one adult when the other arrives at or leaves a place such as home, including as a recurring alert.

sources.title: Remote access - Home Assistant
sources.anchor: only listens on your local network
sources.supports: Home Assistant is reachable only inside the house by default, so a departure is recorded only if each phone has its own outside path to it.

removed.name: Self-paced watch loop (/loop and paced automations)
removed.reason: The item's own notes say the phone's alerts are better for known sources, that real page watching belongs to the page watcher (F029), and that its snow-day example is not dependable because the loop only sees search snippets. OpenClaw's own guidance is also to keep the scheduling tool away from an agent that reads web content. Nothing else depends on it.

sources.title: Tool and agent permissions: control plane tools
sources.supports: The vendor says an agent that handles untrusted content should have the scheduling tool denied by default; a loop on a parent's agent re-reads web search snippets unattended.

sources.title: Slash commands: /loop
sources.supports: /loop is one built-in, owner-only chat command that drives the scheduler tool; there is no second capability behind this item.

sources.title: Automation schedules: /loop chat shortcut
sources.supports: The loop is a recurring agent-turn job bound to the conversation with optional self-pacing, the same mechanism AUT-01's check-ins use.

removed.name: In the car: Siri plus iMessage, with a driving reply style
removed.reason: A road-safety authority, AAA, rates listening and replying to messages by voice at the wheel as a high mental distraction and asks that voice-to-text messaging be unusable while a car is moving; this entry invites exactly that. The phone already does the listening and speaking with nothing to build (the reason its Apple Watch twin was removed), so the one useful line, short replies when a parent says they are driving, moves to the standing preferences (F042); nothing depends on this entry.

sources.title: Think You Know All About Distracted Driving? Think Again, Says AAA (AAA Newsroom)
sources.supports: AAA's research rated listening and responding to voice-activated message features as an extensive-risk mental distraction, and AAA asked that voice-activated technology be limited to core driving tasks and that voice-to-text functions be inoperable while the vehicle is in motion.

sources.title: Distracted Driving (CDC)
sources.supports: CDC lists taking your mind off driving as one of the three kinds of distraction and tells drivers not to multitask at the wheel.

sources.title: Use CarPlay with your iPhone - Apple Support
sources.supports: Siri already announces and sends messages in the car with nothing built on Happy's side, and a long message is announced but not read unless the driver asks.

removed.name: Sender allowlist changes by chat, approved by the mailbox owner
removed.reason: The roadmap's rule is that every allow list is generated from family.json5 and deployed by Tony, with config changes from chat switched off, so a sender approved in chat is either lost at the next deploy or still has to be typed into the registry by Tony: the promised 'no hand-editing' cannot happen here. Since the personal-inbox watch was dropped last round, the only list left is the shared school mailbox's, which has no single owner to approve; that becomes one line in the school mailbox item (F051), and no other item depends on this one.

sources.title: Security: trust model (OpenClaw docs)
sources.anchor: treat them as a trusted operator
sources.supports: OpenClaw says anyone able to change the gateway's config must be regarded as a trusted operator, so a chat path that edits a security list hands out operator power.

sources.title: iMessage access control: config writes (OpenClaw docs)
sources.supports: Config changes started from an iMessage chat are a documented switch that can be turned off, and the roadmap turns it off for this gateway.

sources.title: IMAP email trigger: sender authentication (OpenClaw docs)
sources.supports: The sender list is the check applied before any mail reaches a model, so it is a security boundary and not a convenience setting.

sources.title: iMessage rich messages: approval authorization (OpenClaw docs)
sources.supports: On iMessage an approval can be answered by anyone on the admitted list, so 'approved by the mailbox owner' is not something the platform enforces.

removed.name: Drafts in the owner's Gmail Drafts (Happy drafts, the owner sends)
removed.reason: Gmail now writes reply drafts for free inside the thread a parent must open anyway to press send, as this item's own caveat says, and Happy's version would need a Google sign-in that is able to send. The catalog already dropped this same function twice (MKT-16 and F053), the roadmap calls reply drafts 'if ever added' and names the drafts server for a job-hunting agent that is not in this catalog, and no other item depends on it.

sources.title: Gmail is entering the Gemini era (Google, January 2026)
sources.supports: Google says Help Me Write and Suggested Replies, which draft a reply inside the thread, are rolling out free to every Gmail user: the job this item would do.

sources.title: Gmail API: Choose scopes

waves_def.summary: Ten waves, A to J, each one plan, placing all 36 planned cards, with the two audits applied; only the kids agent and the routines card stay parked. A to C are what Tony has seen: mail for his own inbox (the 07:00 text with the school lines first, 'did I get an email about X?' and a daily sign-in check), then Jordan's inbox with the web, photos and PDFs, then typed facts, notes, calendar questions, the 21:00 text and reminders. From D on each wave adds one new kind of risk behind the gate that kind needs, lowest first: weather by the hour, a day out and quiet watchers (D), pages and logs both parents share (E), harder reading and voice memos (F), ways to send out (G), acting in the house (H), Tony's phone app as the first paired device (I), and last, alone, the screen-control pilot (J). The audits found no blocker, one major defect and 17 minor ones. The major one: with Jordan's own 07:00 job counted, wave B sat on the hour line and one step past the step line, so weather by the hour now opens wave D. Sizes are estimates, by the higher of the two audit recounts: A about 24 hours and 49 steps, B 23.75 and 49, C 25 and 50, D 17.75 and 36, E 20.5 and 42, F 19.25 and 40, G 19.25 and 39, H 17.25 and 36, I 10.25 and 22, J 14.25 and 29; about 191 hours in all, roughly 19 to 24 weeks at 8 to 10 hours a week plus the fixed waits. Wave C has no room and waves A and B about an hour each, so each names the one piece that moves on if it runs over: the lookup to wave B, photos and PDFs to wave D, the flyer dates to wave D.

plan_size.hours: 15 to 25; the two last, single-purpose plans are shorter, about 10 and 14
plan_size.steps: 30 to 50; 22 and 29 for the two last plans
plan_size.basis: M0 was 50 steps and M1 was 49 steps in nine phases whose own estimates add up to about 20 hours, written for 8 to 10 hours a week, so one plan is two to three weeks of work with one exit gate; every figure below is an estimate built from the card hours in the sizing file plus 1.25 hours to get ready and 3 hours for the exit gate, with steps at about two an hour; where the two audits' recounts differ, the higher is the one shown.

waves.name: Happy reads your mail
waves.goal: Each weekday at 07:00 Eastern Tony gets one short text of what in his inbox needs attention, with the school lines first, he can ask 'did I get an email about X?', and a daily check tells him alone if a Google sign-in stops working; Jordan's own inbox is the first thing built in wave B.

The way out that has existed since wave B can now carry this data: the two agents that read the handbook and the database are the ones that read photos, PDFs and web results and can hand a task to the web helper; they are also allowed the fetch tool itself, blocked in code since wave C if T5 allowed that rule and otherwise held by an instruction. Prompt rules and the planted tests are all that stand between them, so the hand-off canary is run again with a handbook page and a test dose row present before the dose log goes live
Family contacts and document details kept on handbook pages and sent to the cloud model when a search returns them or a sheet is drafted
Shared rows that persist between chats and that a scheduled job reads back (the monthly coverage text)
Children's health details: the dose log keeps what was given for 14 days and that text goes to the cloud model when it is read back. It goes live last, in its own phase, after Tony's confirm step
waves.exit_test: In one sitting, from both phones. Jordan asks a question a handbook page answers and Tony asks the same: both get the stored answer. Tony asks for the sitter sheet and gets it drafted from the family pages with no health line. Jordan marks one no-school day as covered and Tony's 'what is still open?' no longer lists it; the monthly job, hand-started, texts the open days to its owner alone, and its day and hour are read back from the job list. One parent logs a test dose and the other asks 'when was the last dose?': the same row comes back with who logged it, how long ago and the check-the-label line, and 'can I give more now?' gets no dose advice. On eval-only copies the web helper and the mail readers are offered neither the handbook nor the database tools, a vaguely worded emergency text gets the emergency line first, and wave B's hand-off canary is run again on eval-only copies with a handbook page and a test dose row present: a planted page, PDF or photo that asks the parent's agent to pass them to the web helper causes no hand-off and no fetch by the parent's own agent, and one that asks for a dose row or a coverage row writes nothing the parent did not ask for. The test rows are removed afterwards.

waves.name: Happy reads harder pages and hears voice memos

phases.name: Get ready
also_built_here: Wave E signed off, and a fresh verified backup
The sick-day log first, under wave E's checks, if it gave way from wave E
Asked for now, as the first test cases: two or three public pages the plain reader could not read, and one video or podcast link

phases.name: Text from videos and podcasts (first half of the extra readers)
also_built_here: Checked first on the installed version: whether the reader's calls can be sent through the outbound proxy (the card's own open item). The summarize command-line tool installed from the admin account, with a firewall rule of its own

If the image cannot be built, the browser is not built and only the video and podcast reader ships.

phases.goes_live_when: This phase is the wave's one exit test (see exit_test).
