notes: Helpers. On 13 Oct Tony chose this shape for the mail lookup ("go with the first version") and said of the helpers still to come: "Not just email reader, we expect to adopt this pattern (Happy main agent hold tools, then dispatch sub-agent to narrow tool selection to do their specific work)". The reason is the platform. On OpenClaw 2026.9.7 an agent started by another keeps only the tools its asker is allowed: the installed code passes the asker's allowed tools and its denies to the helper and applies them last, and no setting turns that off. So in every wave a parent's own agent is allowed the tools of the helpers it starts (the Gmail read tools in A and B, the fetch tool in B, the browser and the video reader in F, the lights and speakers tools in H), is told to hand the work over and never to use those tools itself, and the helper's own shorter list is what narrows each hand-off. Until wave C's house-rules plugin can block a parent's agent in code, which test T5 has to show is possible, that rule is an instruction checked by tool-call records and planted tests; eval-only copies of a parent's agent never hold a connector tool (except T5's throwaway pair in wave C, which reads only the test mailbox). From wave B they do hold the hand-off to eval-only copies of the web helper (in wave H, of the home agent) and the tools those helpers need that are not connectors, so that the planted cases can test a hand-off by its tool-call records (a check on the relayed answer needs the harness to read the asker's follow-up turn, or is made live as wave A's lookup is); the separation check is changed to match when that hand-off is built. The cards and waves were changed to this on 13 Oct; hours and steps were not re-counted.

Base: the 'risk gates first' design. All three judges chose it (their scores for it were 4, 4 and 4; for the dependency-first design 3, 3 and 4; for the use-first design 2, 3 and 3), and none found a blocker in any design. Its three major defects are fixed here: wave A was over one plan, wave A's size was understated, and the last wave held the two highest kinds of risk. Two audits of that merged definition (one on executability, one on the roadmap's rules) then found no blocker, one major defect and 17 minor ones; what was done about each is listed under audit_fixes.

Sizes, all estimates: about 191.25 hours and about 392 steps across the ten waves. That is 146.5 card hours from the sizing file, 4.25 hours of getting ready and exit gate per wave, and about 2.25 hours that the judges and the audits added: half an hour each for Jordan's lookup checks and for her own 07:00 job, a quarter of an hour in wave A's scheduler phase, three quarters of an hour in wave C's try-it-first phase and a quarter of an hour for wave E's planted test. It is roughly 19 to 24 weeks at 8 to 10 hours a week, plus the fixed waits. Where two counts differed, the highest is used. Nothing here has been tried on the Mac.

Move 1, Jordan's inbox: from the last build phase of wave A to the first build phase of wave B. Two of the three judges counted wave A with both inboxes at 25.5 to 25.75 hours and 51 steps, over one plan; the third counted 25.25 hours and said it fits only with her inbox as the piece that gives way. Wave A is now about 24 hours and 49 steps and wave B about 23.75 hours and 49 steps, with her own 07:00 job counted and weather by the hour moved on to wave D. Nothing waits on Jordan: she has agreed, and her 07:00 text is the first thing wave B switches on. Until then Tony's school lines cover the school mail, which both parents receive. The mail card (G015) is counted once, in wave A.

Move 2, the last wave is now two: wave I is the device deny list and the app on Tony's iPhone, wave J is the screen-control pilot alone. The judges disagreed here. The rules judge called one wave with a paired phone and screen control a major defect: the deny list is Gateway-wide, and the phone should have run through a signed-off stretch before two of its entries are lifted. The executability judge called the split optional. The intent judge preferred one wave of about 20 hours, because the pilot alone leaves nothing a parent notices if step zero fails, and two short plans cost two sign-offs. I split, because the roadmap's rule is one new kind of risk per plan where possible and here it is possible. The cost is real: waves I and J are short plans (about 10 and 14 hours), and wave J ends with an answer about one chore, not with a daily feature. If Tony would rather have one plan, I and J merge into one of about 20 hours with the phone first and screen control last, each in its own phases, as two of the three designs drew it. The executability audit puts a number on that cost: between them the two plans' 16 card hours carry 8.5 hours of getting ready and exit gates. It names a second small way to fill wave I, also not done here: move voice memos (F003, 4 hours, no new kind of risk, and the source of the voice Talk mode may use) from wave F to the front of wave I, which gives wave I about 14.25 hours and wave F about 15.25. Both are Tony's call.

The paper pair (the stop-and-check sheet with test T8, and Jordan's half page; 1.5 hours) is counted in wave B, as the base had it, and may be done in wave A's eight-day wait if the first week runs ahead of its hours. All three judges named this graft (from the dependency-first design). When that happens wave A ends as Tony saw it, with the sheet on paper before the first unattended text has run for long.

The day out (F028) stays in wave D, as the base had it, now right after weather by the hour, whose first user it is. The intent judge wanted it as the last build phase of wave B so that it stays inside A to C, giving way to wave D when Jordan's inbox is carried in. Since her inbox is now drawn in wave B, wave B is full and that rule sends the day out to wave D. It was in wave C in the definition Tony saw.

Grafted from the use-first design: (1) wave C opens with 'try it first', T7 then T5, before any rule is written, so a failed T7 frees about 6 hours at the start and not the end; (2) get-ready lines that ask early for what takes a parent time to gather (the family facts and calendar names in C; the page to watch and a first project in D; the school district's calendar, the family-page facts and a short label for each child in E; the hard pages and a video or podcast link in F), each still listed under tony_provides and none holding a wave; (3) the decisions a failed test hands Tony, listed under tony_provides in the wave where the test runs (the day-8 search, T4, T5, T6, T7, the reply check); (4) the reply check in wave A's exit test, with his signature as a condition for the web helper in wave B; (5) the roadmap's trace and attribution levels (O2 and O3) recorded as not carried in waves A and B; (6) the count of scheduled jobs checked in wave D's get-ready; (7) the line that the iPhone app is not the connected idle iPhone Tony once described.

Grafted from the dependency-first design: (1) the house-rules plugin's go-live check in wave C includes both 07:00 mail texts still arriving the next morning; (2) T5 has a turn for the file-write tools, and the plugin is built before 'remember this', so the notes fallback has a plugin to put its rule in; (3) the America/New_York zone is named on the 21:00 job; (4) after the device deny list is deployed, every connector and the helper's browser are checked, not the mail connector alone; (5) the split of the last wave (move 2).

Three checks the rules judge added, tests only, no new mechanism: the video and podcast reader's wrapper is asked the same three home-network questions as wave B's page-fetch path (wave F); after the gateway's process gets the macOS Local Network permission, wave B's home-network refusals and the browser's home-network test are run again (wave H); the shared Reminders list gets one planted page or file that asks for an item to be added (wave G).

Order inside two waves changed so that the piece named to give way is the last build phase (the executability judge's point): in wave G 'email me this' is now built before the group chat, and in wave H switching is built before printing; in wave B the last build phase is now photos and PDFs. Exit tests were widened where the judges found them short of the goal: wave A's is Tony's inbox with the reply check; wave B's adds Jordan's 07:00 text and her own mail question; wave C's adds a real flyer turned into reminders after a yes and both morning mail texts; wave D's has the conflict watch report a second test event from its own scheduled run.

Every card has one home wave, the one it is listed in. 'gives_way_first' names the single piece that moves to the next wave only if that plan runs over its hours, and the next wave's get-ready says where it is then built. A piece that gives way takes its exit-test clause with it: the clause is struck from the wave it leaves and added to the exit test of the wave that builds it. The chain closes: wave A's piece lands in B, B's and C's in D, which is drawn light for them (about 17.75 hours, about 23 with everything they can send), and each later wave has room for the piece before it (E about 24 hours with the conflict watch, F about 23.75 with the sick-day log, G about 23.25 with voice memos, H about 21 with the group chat, I about 14.25 with printing). The 21:00 text is in wave C and moves only in the one case named there.

What changed in A to C against what Tony has seen, and why. Wave A now holds 'did I get an email about X?' and no coded connector check (S1 approved; the lookup is the reading of his answers he did not contradict), and still holds the daily sign-in check (S14). The paper pair is counted in wave B. Jordan's inbox opens wave B; the earlier wave A had it 'only if there is room'. The device deny list left wave B for wave I, where the first device is paired (S14). Weather by the hour left wave B for the front of wave D, because with it wave B was on the hour line and one step past the step line once Jordan's own 07:00 job was counted. The house-rules plugin is created in wave C (about 1.5 hours more there), so the day out moved from C to D. 'Email me this' was a fill-in in C and is in wave G with the other ways to send out. The handbook was 'next in line' for C and is in wave E.

The order after C is by kind of risk, lowest first, which is the roadmap's rule, not a guess about what the family will use most; Tony has not said which features Jordan would use. Wave D is mostly for Tony (the weekly text, the page watch and the check-ins are his only), while wave E is the first that both parents notice every week. No card in D depends on a card in E or the other way round, so the two can swap at his word; if they do, what gives way from waves B and C still goes to the plan that holds wave D's cards and waits one plan longer, because wave E has no room for all of it. F and G can swap the same way; the cost is running the injected-page recipient test again when the browser arrives. Not grafted: the use-first design's order after C, for that reason.

Also not grafted: moving the daily sign-in check out of wave A (all three judges want it with mail), and moving voice memos beside the phone app (the rules judge allowed either place; they stay in wave F, where both parents get them sooner).

Mail runs on one layer from wave A until wave C's plugin phase: tool permissions, an explicit deny and two tests, without the roadmap's coded check on who may call the connector. That is the approved S1. Since 13 Oct it describes the layer between the two parents; between a parent's own agent and its own mail reader there is no tool limit once the lookup is on, only an instruction and a count of tool calls, because that agent is allowed the reader's tools. T5's connector turn at the start of wave C decides whether the rule can be written at all, and whether its second half can (the check must be told which agent is calling); if it cannot, Tony decides then whether one layer is enough for the calendar too.

The riskiest combination in A to C appears at the end of wave B: a parent's own agent then holds private chat and mail answers, reads photos and PDFs directly, and can hand a task to a helper that fetches any public address; since 13 Oct it is also allowed the fetch tool and the Gmail read tools themselves, for its helpers' sake. Only a prompt rule and planted tests stand between them; the roadmap calls that hand-off its one remaining leak path. Tony signs it in wave B's exit gate. The harder line, if he ever wants it, is to switch the lookup off. From wave E the same two agents also read the handbook pages and the dose log, so wave E runs the hand-off canary again with those present and Tony signs the line there too.

Tests that can end or shrink a card, each placed where its answer is first needed: T1 (day 8, wave A: a weekly sign-in or a different connector); T4 (waves A, B and H: the only documented fix changes a signed-off setting); T5 (waves C, F, G and H: a rule that cannot see its fields, or cannot tell which agent is calling, cannot be written); T6 (wave C: the fallback reverses two signed-off settings and needs Tony's yes; its shared-folder part again in wave E); T7 (wave C: if a reminder cannot be created from iMessage, reminders, flyer dates and project check-ins are not built and Tony decides what comes next); T9 (wave G: the shared-list card is dropped and recipe ingredients come back as text); the browser image build (wave F); step zero (wave J). T2 is in A, B and C, T3 in A and D, T8 in B. T10 is in no wave: its only user, an envelope for Jordan, is not planned.

What works for Jordan and what does not. She gets the 07:00 mail text and the lookup (wave B), web answers, photos and PDFs, notes, calendar questions, the handbook, the grid, the dose log, voice memos, the shared list, 'email me this', the group chat, lights and printing. She is not a command owner, so timed reminders, flyer reminders and project check-ins are Tony's only, and her copies of the evening text, the conflict watch, the weekly text and the monthly coverage text are separate jobs that Tony says are switched on at execution. Nothing is ever sent from one parent's Happy into the other parent's chat.

Children's data. From wave C the two children's first names, school years and school district go to the cloud model with every chat of a parent's own agent. From wave E the dose log keeps what was given for 14 days and sends it to the cloud model when read back, on Tony's confirm step. Web searches and helper tasks may carry the town and ages, never names or the school, which is a prompt rule checked by a canary, not an enforced limit. The kids agent stays parked.

Roadmap lines that are not carried, each by Tony's own answer, an approved simplification or because nothing can act on it: a local model for mail (cloud model with the Zero Data Retention application filed); the blocking firewall and proxy before mail (answer 7a: one rule first); the prompt-injection tripwire (answer 7c: waits for local models); the trace and attribution levels O2 and O3 (local models were skipped; only the keeping of the mail readers' records is carried, and the wave A runbook found that it is not a 30-day deletion: Tony signs what OpenClaw keeps, or switches on an optional setting, at its step A4); the secret egress proxy (nothing for it to act on); groups disabled (re-opened for one chat in wave G); one data domain per person (the handbook, the database and busy-only calendar sharing are shared on purpose, and he signs the first two as a departure in wave E). Two more lines are met only in part. 'Anything that acts ends with you pressing the button': in wave H lights, speakers and printing act on a parent's text with no approval step, so the line is met only by the parent's own message, and inside the limits in code (named rooms and scenes, favourites, the volume cap, one queue, the copies cap) a planted instruction is held back by a prompt rule and the planted tests, not by code; acting in the house is also not the last wave, because the phone app and screen control follow it. And one of Tony's own earlier decisions, alerts by ntfy: from wave A a failed scheduled job alerts him by a text from Happy, because the other route would post the raw error text to an outside push service. Nothing on the never list is added in any wave, every scheduled text goes only to its owner, and no agent sends into another person's conversation.

Scheduled jobs: by wave H the jobs script holds eight texts (two mail texts, each of which the wave A runbook builds as two jobs, the evening text, the weekly text, the page watch, the conflict watch, the monthly coverage text and the 'still on' check), and more with Jordan's copies. The approved S9 says the comparing step is built when the list can no longer be read at a glance; no wave counts hours for it. Every job's target keeps coming from the family file. S9's comparing step is not the name-keyed comparison the scheduler card keeps if T3 shows that a job added twice is doubled: that one is written in wave A's scheduler phase, about an hour.

Waves I and J, one thing to know: the deny list is Gateway-wide, so lifting the two entries for the screen-control pilot lifts them for Tony's paired phone too. The phone's command list is read again first, and Tony decides before anything is lifted. Until wave I nothing in config covers a device paired by mistake; the written rule meanwhile is no Mac app, no pairing and no setup code, and the one documented line against screen control can ride along in any earlier deploy if he wants a visible 'no' sooner. At wave J's exit gate the guest's pairing is revoked and its route to the gateway closed, unless Tony signs that they stay, so the phone is again the only paired device.

Fixed waits that set the calendar: day 8 of the Google sign-in in A; one night of the proxy in report mode and a day between the two parents' agents in B; two-day exit tests in C and D; one evening in H.

Unverified: every hour and step figure; the splits of F020, F076, OCL-01 and MAC-02 into phases; the half hour for Jordan's lookup checks and the half hour for her own 07:00 job; the audits' recounts of wave A's scheduler phase and wave C's try-it-first phase; whether the video and podcast reader can send its calls through the outbound proxy; and everything the cards themselves list as not tried, in particular the connector's flags (it is not installed), whether a blocking check sees connector, scheduling, file-write, browser, send and in-house lights and speakers calls, and whether it is told which agent is calling, whether a command job can use a stored calendar sign-in, and whether screen control works inside a virtual Mac at all.

Missing details never hold a wave: each is listed under tony_provides for the wave that uses it. What can still change a plan is a test result at execution, each with the fallback its card names. The only items that wait for something outside the plan are the two parked cards.

Against the earlier definition (three waves and 23 items left out, written before Tony's answers): 'changes_from_before' lists every planned card whose wave changed, and the mail card, whose wave is the same while its two halves moved. Four items of that definition are no longer cards, each dropped by an approved simplification: the notification-policy plugin (G001, S4), texts into the other parent's chat (G009, S5), the renewals table (F063, S11) and the outage notice (CRT-04, S14). The kids agent (F072) and the routines card (AUT-06) were not in a wave then and are not now.

changes_from_before.why: Still wave A, but its halves moved: 'did I get an email about X?' is now built in wave A (the coded connector check waits for wave C under the approved S1), and Jordan's inbox is the first build phase of wave B, because both inboxes do not fit one plan.
The printed stop-and-check sheet with test T8 is counted in wave B, where it fills the proxy's night in report mode; wave A has no hours for it, though it may be done in wave A's eight-day wait.
